steps: Write out the formula and identify every atom present
Look up each Ar value and multiply by the number of atoms (watch brackets!)
Add them all up to get Mr
To find moles: divide mass by Mr. To find mass: multiply moles by Mr
State your answer with the correct unit (no unit for Mr, mol for moles, g for mass, % for composition)
method_card.title: Relative Formula Mass and Moles
method_card.content:
These calculations underpin every chemistry calculation you will meet at GCSE. If you can't do these quickly and accurately, multi-step problems become very difficult.

Approach:

  • To find \(M_r\), add up every atom's \(A_r\) — don't forget subscripts and brackets
  • Brackets multiply everything inside: Ca(OH)₂ means 2 × O and 2 × H
  • Moles links mass to formula mass — rearrange the triangle depending on what you need
  • Percentage composition asks what fraction of the total mass comes from one element

Common pitfalls:

  • Forgetting to multiply inside brackets — Ca(OH)₂ has 2 oxygen atoms, not 1
  • Using the wrong \(A_r\) value — double-check the periodic table
  • Confusing moles and mass — moles is a count, mass is in grams
  • For percentage composition, divide by the total \(M_r\), not just part of it

exam_context.frequency: Every exam — Mr and moles appear on every Paper 1

gold.display: Calculate the percentage by mass of calcium in calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. (\(A_r\): Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Remember to multiply by 100 to convert the fraction to a percentage.

gold.display: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in potassium nitrate, KNO₃. Give your answer to 1 d.p. (\(A_r\): K = 39, N = 14, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Make sure you're finding the percentage of nitrogen (Ar = 14), not potassium or oxygen.

gold.display: Calculate the percentage by mass of oxygen in water, H₂O. Give your answer to 1 d.p. (\(A_r\): H = 1, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: The question asks for oxygen, not hydrogen. % O = (16 ÷ 18) × 100 = 88.9%.

gold.display: A sample of a compound contains 0.1 mol and has a mass of 7.1 g. Calculate the relative formula mass of the compound.

misconceptions.message: Mr = mass ÷ moles = 7.1 ÷ 0.1 = 71. Rearrange moles = mass ÷ Mr to find Mr.
Rearrange: if moles = mass ÷ Mr, then Mr = mass ÷ moles = 7.1 ÷ 0.1 = 71.

gold.display: A scientist has 0.05 mol of a compound with a mass of 4.9 g. Calculate the \(M_r\) of the compound and suggest its identity. (\(M_r\): H₂SO₄ = 98, HNO₃ = 63, HCl = 36.5, NaOH = 40)

misconceptions.message: Mr = mass ÷ moles = 4.9 ÷ 0.05 = 98. This matches H₂SO₄.
Rearrange: Mr = mass ÷ moles = 4.9 ÷ 0.05 = 98.

gold.display: Calculate the mass of 3 mol of carbon dioxide, CO₂. (\(A_r\): C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Mass = moles × Mr = 3 × 44 = 132 g. Multiply, don't divide.

bronze.display: Calculate the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of sodium chloride, NaCl. (\(A_r\): Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)

misconceptions.message: Check your Ar values. Na = 23 and Cl = 35.5, so Mr = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5.

bronze.display: Calculate the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of water, H₂O. (\(A_r\): H = 1, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: There are 2 hydrogen atoms in H₂O. Mr = 2 × 1 + 16 = 18.

bronze.display: Calculate the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of carbon dioxide, CO₂. (\(A_r\): C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: CO₂ has 2 oxygen atoms. Mr = 12 + 2 × 16 = 12 + 32 = 44.

bronze.display: Calculate the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. (\(A_r\): Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: CaCO₃ has 3 oxygen atoms. Mr = 40 + 12 + 3 × 16 = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100.

bronze.display: Calculate the number of moles in 36 g of water, H₂O. (\(M_r\) of H₂O = 18)

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 36 ÷ 18 = 2 mol. Don't multiply — divide.

bronze.display: Calculate the number of moles in 5.5 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂. (\(M_r\) of CO₂ = 44)

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 5.5 ÷ 44 = 0.125 mol.

bronze.display: Calculate the number of moles in 4.8 g of magnesium oxide, MgO. (\(M_r\) of MgO = 40)

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 4.8 ÷ 40 = 0.12 mol.

bronze.display: Calculate the mass of 0.5 mol of water, H₂O. (\(M_r\) of H₂O = 18)

misconceptions.message: Mass = moles × Mr = 0.5 × 18 = 9 g. Multiply, don't divide.

silver.display: Calculate the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂. (\(A_r\): Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: The bracket means 2 × (O + H) = 2 × (16 + 1) = 34. Mr = 40 + 34 = 74.
Ca(OH)₂ has TWO OH groups. Mr = 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74, not 57.

silver.display: Calculate the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO₃)₂. (\(A_r\): Mg = 24, N = 14, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: The bracket multiplies everything inside by 2: 2 × (14 + 3 × 16) = 2 × 62 = 124. Mr = 24 + 124 = 148.

silver.display: Calculate the number of moles in 11.7 g of sodium chloride, NaCl. (\(M_r\) of NaCl = 58.5)

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 11.7 ÷ 58.5 = 0.2 mol.

silver.display: Calculate the number of moles in 25 g of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. (\(M_r\) of CaCO₃ = 100)

misconceptions.message: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 mol.

silver.display: Calculate the mass of 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. (\(M_r\) of CaCO₃ = 100)

misconceptions.message: Mass = moles × Mr = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g. Multiply, don't divide.

silver.display: Calculate the mass of 0.4 mol of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃. (\(A_r\): Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)

steps.label: Step 1 — Identify the atoms
steps.content: MgO contains 1 magnesium atom and 1 oxygen atom.

worked_examples.question: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of magnesium oxide, MgO. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)
Calculate the number of moles in 14.8 g of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂. (Ar: Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1)

steps.label: Step 2 — Find the mass contribution of iron

worked_examples.question: Calculate the percentage by mass of iron in iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃. (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16)

steps: Write or check the balanced equation — get the mole ratio
Calculate the moles of the substance you know (moles = mass ÷ Mr)
Use the mole ratio to find the moles of the substance you want
Convert back to mass if needed (mass = moles × Mr)
State your answer with the correct unit
method_card.title: Balancing Equations and Reacting Masses
method_card.content:
Reacting mass questions follow a fixed four-step method every time. Master the method and you can tackle any question — the chemistry changes, but the maths never does.

Approach:

  • Always start from a balanced equation — the big numbers in front of formulae tell you the mole ratio
  • The mole ratio is the bridge between two substances — it tells you how many moles of product you get from a given number of moles of reactant
  • If the question gives you a mass, convert to moles first. If it asks for a mass, convert from moles at the end.

Common pitfalls:

  • Using an unbalanced equation — the ratio will be wrong and your answer will be wrong
  • Confusing the coefficients (big numbers) with subscripts (small numbers)
  • Forgetting to convert between moles and mass at the start and end
  • Using the \(M_r\) of the wrong substance when converting back to mass
  • In limiting reactant problems, always check both reactants — the one that runs out first limits the product

exam_context.frequency: Almost every exam — a common 4–5 mark multi-step question

gold.display: 6.5 g of zinc reacts with excess hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. The mass of ZnCl₂ produced is 13.6 g. Calculate the mass of hydrogen gas produced using conservation of mass. (The total mass of HCl used is 7.3 g.)

misconceptions.message: Conservation of mass: total reactants = total products. (6.5 + 7.3) = (13.6 + H₂). H₂ = 13.8 − 13.6 = 0.2 g.
You don't need Mr here — just use conservation of mass. Reactant mass in = product mass out.

gold.display: 12 g of magnesium reacts with 12 g of oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Which is the limiting reactant? Enter Mg or O₂.

misconceptions.message: Moles Mg = 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5. Moles O₂ = 12 ÷ 32 = 0.375. Ratio: 2 Mg needs 1 O₂, so 0.5 mol Mg needs 0.25 mol O₂. We have 0.375 mol O₂ — enough. Mg is limiting because all 0.5 mol is used up.

gold.display: 12 g of magnesium reacts with 12 g of oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Calculate the mass of MgO formed. (\(A_r\): Mg = 24, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Use the limiting reactant (Mg). Moles Mg = 0.5. Ratio 2:2 → 0.5 mol MgO. Mass = 0.5 × 40 = 20 g.

gold.display: In the reaction 2Al + 3CuSO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3Cu, a student reacts 2.7 g of aluminium with excess copper sulfate solution. Calculate the mass of copper produced. (\(A_r\): Al = 27, Cu = 64)

misconceptions.message: The ratio is 2:3, not 1:1. Multiply moles of Al by 3/2 to get moles of Cu.

gold.display: Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. 6.5 g of zinc is added to excess acid. Calculate the volume of hydrogen gas produced at room temperature and pressure, where 1 mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³. (\(A_r\): Zn = 65, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Moles of Zn = 6.5 ÷ 65 = 0.1. Ratio 1:1. Moles H₂ = 0.1. Volume = 0.1 × 24 = 2.4 dm³.
Mr of Zn = 65 (not 64, that's copper). Moles = 6.5 ÷ 65 = 0.1.

gold.display: Calcium reacts with water: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. Calculate the mass of calcium hydroxide produced from 4 g of calcium. (\(A_r\): Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Ca(OH)₂ has Mr = 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74, not 57. Don't forget to multiply the bracket.

bronze.display: Balance this equation: Na + Cl₂ → NaCl. What number goes in front of Na?

misconceptions.message: Cl₂ has 2 chlorine atoms but NaCl has only 1. You need 2NaCl, which means you also need 2Na. Answer: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.

bronze.display: Balance this equation: Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃. What number goes in front of Fe?

misconceptions.message: Balanced equation: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃. Check: 4 Fe each side, 6 O each side.

bronze.display: Balance this equation: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O. What number goes in front of H₂?

misconceptions.message: Balanced: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Check: 4 H each side, 2 O each side.

bronze.display: In the equation 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, what is the mole ratio of Mg to MgO?

misconceptions.message: The coefficients are 2Mg and 2MgO. The ratio is 2:2, which simplifies to 1:1. Both '1:1' and '2:2' are correct.

bronze.display: In the equation N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, how many moles of NH₃ are produced from 1 mol of N₂?

misconceptions.message: The ratio of N₂ to NH₃ is 1:2. So 1 mol N₂ produces 2 mol NH₃.

bronze.display: In the equation CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, how many moles of CO₂ are produced from 3 mol of CaCO₃?

misconceptions.message: The ratio is 1:1. So 3 mol CaCO₃ produces 3 mol CO₂.

bronze.display: 4.8 g of magnesium reacts with oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Calculate the mass of MgO produced. (\(A_r\): Mg = 24, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Moles of Mg = 4.8 ÷ 24 = 0.2. Ratio 2:2 (1:1), so 0.2 mol MgO. Mr of MgO = 40. Mass = 0.2 × 40 = 8 g.
Use Mr of MgO (= 40) to convert moles of MgO to mass, not Mr of Mg.

bronze.display: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Calculate the mass of hydrogen gas produced from 2.4 g of magnesium. (\(A_r\): Mg = 24, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Moles Mg = 2.4 ÷ 24 = 0.1. Ratio 1:1. Mr of H₂ = 2. Mass = 0.1 × 2 = 0.2 g.
Use Mr of H₂ (= 2) to convert moles of H₂ to mass.

silver.display: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Calculate the mass of CO₂ produced from 25 g of CaCO₃. (\(A_r\): Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Mr of CaCO₃ = 100, Mr of CO₂ = 44. Moles = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25. Ratio 1:1. Mass = 0.25 × 44 = 11 g.
Convert to moles using Mr of CaCO₃ (100), then convert back using Mr of CO₂ (44).

silver.display: Sodium reacts with water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Calculate the mass of NaOH produced from 4.6 g of sodium. (\(A_r\): Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Moles of Na = 4.6 ÷ 23 = 0.2. Ratio Na:NaOH = 2:2 = 1:1. Mr of NaOH = 40. Mass = 0.2 × 40 = 8 g.

silver.display: Iron(III) oxide is reduced: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the mass of iron produced from 32 g of Fe₂O₃. (\(A_r\): Fe = 56, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Moles Fe₂O₃ = 32 ÷ 160 = 0.2. Ratio 1:2. Moles Fe = 0.4. Mass = 0.4 × 56 = 22.4 g.
Mr of Fe₂O₃ = 2 × 56 + 3 × 16 = 160. Mr of Fe = 56 (it's just the element).

silver.display: Aluminium reacts with copper sulfate: 2Al + 3CuSO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3Cu. Calculate the mass of copper produced from 5.4 g of aluminium. (\(A_r\): Al = 27, Cu = 64)

misconceptions.message: Moles of Al = 5.4 ÷ 27 = 0.2. Ratio Al:Cu = 2:3. Moles Cu = 0.2 × 3 ÷ 2 = 0.3. Mass = 0.3 × 64 = 19.2 g.
The ratio is 2 Al : 3 Cu. So multiply moles of Al by 3/2 to get moles of Cu.

silver.display: Nitrogen reacts with hydrogen: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Calculate the mass of ammonia (NH₃) produced from 5.6 g of nitrogen. (\(A_r\): N = 14, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Mr of N₂ = 28, Mr of NH₃ = 17. Moles N₂ = 5.6 ÷ 28 = 0.2. Ratio 1:2. Moles NH₃ = 0.4. Mass = 0.4 × 17 = 6.8 g.

silver.display: Copper oxide reacts with sulfuric acid: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. Calculate the mass of copper sulfate (CuSO₄) produced from 16 g of CuO. (\(A_r\): Cu = 64, O = 16, S = 32, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Mr of CuO = 80, Mr of CuSO₄ = 160. Moles CuO = 16 ÷ 80 = 0.2. Ratio 1:1. Mass CuSO₄ = 0.2 × 160 = 32 g.

steps.label: Step 1 — Count atoms on each side
steps.content: Left: 1 Mg, 2 O. Right: 1 Mg, 1 O. Oxygen is unbalanced.

steps.label: Step 2 — Balance oxygen
steps.content: Put a 2 in front of MgO → Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Now right has 2 Mg, so balance Mg too.

worked_examples.question: Balance this equation: Mg + O₂ → MgO
Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Calculate the mass of calcium oxide (CaO) produced from 25 g of CaCO₃. (Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)

steps.label: Step 1 — Find moles of each reactant
steps.content: Moles of Mg = 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5 mol. Moles of O₂ = 12 ÷ 32 = 0.375 mol.

steps.label: Step 2 — Use the ratio to check which runs out
steps.content:
Ratio is 2 Mg : 1 O₂. So 0.5 mol Mg needs 0.25 mol O₂. We have 0.375 mol O₂ — plenty.

0.375 mol O₂ would need 0.75 mol Mg. We only have 0.5 mol Mg — Mg is limiting.

steps.label: Step 3 — Calculate product from limiting reactant
steps.content: 0.5 mol Mg → 0.5 mol MgO (2:2 ratio). Mass = 0.5 × 40

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Mg is the limiting reactant. Mass of MgO = 20 g

worked_examples.question: 12 g of magnesium reacts with 12 g of oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Which reactant is the limiting reactant? Calculate the mass of MgO formed. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)

steps: Draw out structural formulae and count every bond in reactants and products
Add up the total energy to break all bonds in the reactants
Add up the total energy released when all bonds in the products are made
Calculate: energy change = bonds broken − bonds made
State the sign and whether the reaction is exothermic (−) or endothermic (+)
method_card.title: Bond Energy Calculations
method_card.content:
Bond energy calculations tell you the overall energy change of a reaction. The method is always the same: add up the energy needed to break bonds, subtract the energy released when new bonds form.

Approach:

  • Draw out the structural formulae of all reactants and products — this lets you count every bond
  • Breaking bonds is endothermic (takes energy in). Making bonds is exothermic (gives energy out).
  • If the answer is negative, more energy is released than absorbed — the reaction is exothermic
  • If the answer is positive, more energy is absorbed than released — the reaction is endothermic

Common pitfalls:

  • Miscounting bonds — especially in combustion reactions (count ALL C–H bonds in the fuel, ALL O=O bonds, ALL C=O and O–H bonds in the products)
  • Subtracting the wrong way round — it's always broken minus made
  • Forgetting to multiply bond energies by the number of bonds (e.g. 4 × C–H in CH₄, not just 1)
  • Confusing the sign: negative = exothermic, positive = endothermic

exam_context.frequency: Common — often appears as a 4–5 mark structured question

gold.display: Calculate the overall energy change for the combustion of ethene: C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O. Bond energies: C=C = 614, C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 803, O–H = 464 kJ/mol.

misconceptions.message: C₂H₄ has 4 C–H bonds (2 on each carbon) and 1 C=C bond.

gold.display: Calculate the overall energy change for the combustion of ethane: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. Bond energies: C–C = 347, C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 803, O–H = 464 kJ/mol. Give the answer per mole of C₂H₆ (divide your total by 2).

misconceptions.message: The equation uses 2 mol of C₂H₆, so divide your total ΔH by 2 to get the answer per mole.

gold.display: The overall energy change for a reaction is −285 kJ/mol. The total energy to break bonds in the reactants is 1845 kJ. Calculate the total energy released when new bonds form in the products.

misconceptions.message: ΔH = broken − made. Rearrange: made = broken − ΔH = 1845 − (−285) = 1845 + 285 = 2130 kJ.
Be careful with the negative sign. Subtracting −285 means adding 285.

gold.display: A reaction has ΔH = +140 kJ/mol. The energy released forming product bonds is 1380 kJ. Calculate the total energy needed to break all reactant bonds.

misconceptions.message: ΔH = broken − made. Rearrange: broken = ΔH + made = 140 + 1380 = 1520 kJ.

gold.display: Reaction A has ΔH = −184 kJ/mol. Reaction B has ΔH = −814 kJ/mol. Which reaction releases more energy per mole? Enter A or B.

misconceptions.message: −814 is more negative than −184, so Reaction B releases more energy. A larger negative number means more exothermic.
Compare the size (magnitude) of the negative values: 814 > 184, so B releases more energy.

gold.display: Methane combustion (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O) has ΔH = −814 kJ/mol. Hydrogen combustion (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O) has ΔH = −486 kJ/mol. Which fuel releases more energy per gram? (\(M_r\): CH₄ = 16, H₂ = 2). Enter CH₄ or H₂.

misconceptions.message: Per gram of CH₄: 814 ÷ 16 = 50.9 kJ/g. Per gram of H₂: 486 ÷ (2 × 2) = 486 ÷ 4 = 121.5 kJ/g. H₂ releases more energy per gram, even though CH₄ releases more per mole.

bronze.display: Calculate the total energy needed to break all bonds in the reactants for: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies: H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242 kJ/mol.
bronze.equation_hint: \(\text{total broken} = \text{sum of all bond energies in reactants}\)

misconceptions.message: Only add up bonds in the REACTANTS (left side). Broken = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ.

bronze.display: Calculate the total energy released when all bonds are made in the products for: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies: H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol.
bronze.equation_hint: \(\text{total made} = \text{sum of all bond energies in products}\)

misconceptions.message: There are 2 HCl molecules, so 2 × H–Cl bonds. Total made = 2 × 431 = 862 kJ.

bronze.display: Calculate the overall energy change (ΔH) for: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies: H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242, H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol.

misconceptions.message: ΔH = broken − made = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol. Don't subtract the other way round.
The answer is negative (−184), meaning the reaction is exothermic.

bronze.display: Is the reaction H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl exothermic or endothermic? (ΔH = −184 kJ/mol)

misconceptions.message: A negative ΔH means exothermic — more energy is released making new bonds than is absorbed breaking old ones.

bronze.display: Calculate the overall energy change for: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Bond energies: H–H = 436, O=O = 498, O–H = 464 kJ/mol.

misconceptions.message: 2H₂O has 4 O–H bonds (2 in each water molecule). Total made = 4 × 464 = 1856 kJ.

bronze.display: Calculate the overall energy change for: H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr. Bond energies: H–H = 436, Br–Br = 193, H–Br = 366 kJ/mol.
Calculate the overall energy change for: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Bond energies: N≡N = 945, H–H = 436, N–H = 391 kJ/mol.

misconceptions.message: Broken: 1 × N≡N + 3 × H–H = 945 + 1308 = 2253 kJ. Made: 6 × N–H = 2346 kJ (2 NH₃ molecules, 3 N–H bonds each). ΔH = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ/mol.
2NH₃ has 6 N–H bonds total (3 per molecule × 2 molecules).

bronze.display: In the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how many O–H bonds are formed in total?
bronze.equation_hint: \(\text{count all bonds in all product molecules}\)

misconceptions.message: There are 2 water molecules, each with 2 O–H bonds. Total = 2 × 2 = 4 O–H bonds.
Don't confuse the number of molecules with the number of bonds. 2H₂O = 2 molecules × 2 bonds each = 4 bonds.

silver.display: Calculate the overall energy change for the combustion of methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Bond energies: C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 803, O–H = 464 kJ/mol.

misconceptions.message: 2H₂O has 4 O–H bonds, not 2. Each water molecule has 2 O–H bonds.

silver.display: The combustion of methane (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O) has ΔH = −814 kJ/mol. The total energy to break all bonds in the reactants is 2648 kJ. Calculate the total energy released when bonds in the products are formed.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: bonds made = bonds broken − ΔH = 2648 − (−814) = 2648 + 814 = 3462 kJ.

silver.display: A reaction has bonds broken = 1845 kJ and bonds made = 2130 kJ. Calculate ΔH and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

misconceptions.message: ΔH = 1845 − 2130 = −285 kJ/mol. Negative = exothermic.
More energy is released making bonds (2130 kJ) than absorbed breaking them (1845 kJ), so it's exothermic (negative).

silver.display: A reaction has bonds broken = 1520 kJ and bonds made = 1380 kJ. Calculate ΔH and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

misconceptions.message: ΔH = 1520 − 1380 = +140 kJ/mol. Positive = endothermic — more energy absorbed than released.

silver.display: Calculate the overall energy change for the combustion of hydrogen: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Bond energies: H–H = 436, O=O = 498, O–H = 464 kJ/mol. How many O–H bonds are formed in total?
silver.equation_hint: \(\text{count all bonds in all product molecules}\)

misconceptions.message: 2H₂O means two water molecules. Each has 2 O–H bonds, so 2 × 2 = 4 O–H bonds total.

silver.display: A student calculates ΔH for a reaction and gets +320 kJ/mol. Which statement is correct?
options: More energy is released making bonds than breaking bonds
More energy is absorbed breaking bonds than making bonds
The reaction gives out heat to the surroundings
The products are at a lower energy level than the reactants

misconceptions.message: Positive ΔH means more energy is absorbed breaking bonds than released making them. The reaction is endothermic — it takes in heat from the surroundings.

worked_examples.question: Calculate the overall energy change for: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies: H–H = 436 kJ/mol, Cl–Cl = 242 kJ/mol, H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol.

steps.label: Step 1 — Bonds broken
steps.content:
CH₄: 4 × C–H = 4 × 413 = 1652 kJ
2O₂: 2 × O=O = 2 × 498 = 996 kJ
Total broken = 2648 kJ

steps.label: Step 2 — Bonds made
steps.content:
CO₂: 2 × C=O = 2 × 803 = 1606 kJ
2H₂O: 4 × O–H = 4 × 464 = 1856 kJ
Total made = 3462 kJ

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: ΔH = −814 kJ/mol (exothermic — more energy released making bonds than absorbed breaking them)

worked_examples.question: Calculate the overall energy change for the combustion of methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Bond energies: C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 803, O–H = 464 kJ/mol.

steps.label: Step 1 — Bonds broken
steps.content:
C₂H₄: 1 × C=C = 614, 4 × C–H = 1652. Total = 2266 kJ
3O₂: 3 × O=O = 1494 kJ
Total broken = 3760 kJ

steps.label: Step 2 — Bonds made
steps.content:
2CO₂: 4 × C=O = 3212 kJ
2H₂O: 4 × O–H = 1856 kJ
Total made = 5068 kJ

worked_examples.question: Calculate the energy change for the combustion of ethene: C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O. Bond energies: C=C = 614, C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 803, O–H = 464 kJ/mol.

steps: Identify what quantity is changing (volume, mass, concentration) and read the values
Find the change in quantity and the time period
Calculate: rate = change in quantity ÷ time
For concentration: check whether volume is in dm³ or cm³ (÷ 1000 to convert)
State your answer with the correct unit (e.g. cm³/s, g/s, g/dm³)
method_card.title: Rates from Graphs and Concentrations
method_card.content:
Rate of reaction questions test whether you can extract data from graphs and apply a simple formula. The maths is straightforward — the challenge is reading the graph accurately and converting units correctly.

Approach:

  • Mean rate is always change in quantity divided by time — whether the quantity is volume of gas, mass lost, or amount of product formed
  • For graphs, read values carefully from the axes — don't estimate if you can read exactly
  • The steeper the curve, the faster the reaction. A flat line means the reaction has finished.
  • Concentration is mass per unit volume — but watch whether the volume is in dm³ or cm³

Common pitfalls:

  • Not converting cm³ to dm³ for concentration (divide by 1000)
  • Reading the wrong axis on a graph
  • Confusing initial rate (steepest part at the start) with mean rate (total change ÷ total time)
  • Forgetting units — rate must have a unit of quantity per unit of time

exam_context.frequency: Common — rate graphs appear frequently on Paper 2

gold.display: The graph shows two reactions using the same chemicals. Calculate the mean rate of Reaction A over the first 10 seconds.

misconceptions.message: Read Reaction A (red line). At 10 s, volume = 24 cm³. Rate = 24 ÷ 10 = 2.4 cm³/s.
Use only the first 10 seconds, not the total time.

gold.display: Using the same graph, calculate the mean rate of Reaction B over the first 10 seconds.

misconceptions.message: Read Reaction B (blue line). At 10 s, volume = 15 cm³. Rate = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 cm³/s.

gold.display: Both reactions produce the same total volume (58 cm³). Suggest why Reaction A has a higher initial rate than Reaction B. Which factor could explain this?
options: Reaction A used a higher concentration of acid
Reaction A used a different acid
Reaction A was carried out at a lower temperature

misconceptions.message: Same total volume means same amount of reactant was used. A higher initial rate but same final volume is best explained by higher concentration (more frequent collisions at the start, but same total moles of reactant).

gold.display: A solution has a concentration of 40 g/dm³. A student needs 8 g of solute. Calculate the volume of solution they need in cm³.

misconceptions.message: Volume = mass ÷ concentration = 8 ÷ 40 = 0.2 dm³. Convert to cm³: 0.2 × 1000 = 200 cm³.
Rearrange concentration = mass ÷ volume to get volume = mass ÷ concentration.

gold.display: Use the graph. Calculate the overall mean rate for the entire reaction (from 0 s until the reaction finishes at 60 s).

misconceptions.message: The reaction finishes at 60 s (where the line goes flat at 42 cm³). Mean rate = 42 ÷ 60 = 0.7 cm³/s.
The reaction finishes at 60 s, not 70 s. The line is flat from 60 to 70 — no more gas is produced. Rate = 42 ÷ 60 = 0.7 cm³/s.

gold.display: A hydrochloric acid solution has a concentration of 36 g/dm³. A student uses 500 cm³ of this solution. Calculate the mass of HCl dissolved in this volume.

misconceptions.message: Convert 500 cm³ to dm³: 500 ÷ 1000 = 0.5 dm³. Mass = concentration × volume = 36 × 0.5 = 18 g.
Rearrange: mass = concentration × volume = 36 × 0.5 = 18 g.

bronze.display: A reaction produces 48 cm³ of gas in 60 seconds. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.

misconceptions.message: Rate = quantity ÷ time = 48 ÷ 60 = 0.8 cm³/s. Don't divide time by quantity.

bronze.display: A reaction produces 35 cm³ of gas in 50 seconds. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.

misconceptions.message: Rate = 35 ÷ 50 = 0.7 cm³/s.

bronze.display: In a reaction, the mass of a flask decreases by 0.72 g over 120 seconds as gas escapes. Calculate the mean rate of mass loss.
10 g of salt is dissolved in 2 dm³ of water. Calculate the concentration.

misconceptions.message: Concentration = mass ÷ volume = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 g/dm³.

bronze.display: 4 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in 0.5 dm³ of water. Calculate the concentration.

misconceptions.message: Concentration = mass ÷ volume = 4 ÷ 0.5 = 8 g/dm³.

bronze.display: A reaction produces 56 cm³ of gas in 40 seconds. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.

misconceptions.message: Rate = 56 ÷ 40 = 1.4 cm³/s.

bronze.display: Use the graph. What is the total volume of gas produced by the end of the reaction?
bronze.equation_hint: \(\text{read the final volume from the graph}\)

misconceptions.message: The graph levels off at 42 cm³ (from 60 s onwards). This is the total volume produced.

bronze.display: 20 g of copper sulfate is dissolved in 0.4 dm³ of water. Calculate the concentration.

misconceptions.message: Concentration = mass ÷ volume = 20 ÷ 0.4 = 50 g/dm³.

silver.display: Use the graph. Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 20 seconds.

misconceptions.message: At 20 s, volume = 22 cm³. Rate = 22 ÷ 20 = 1.1 cm³/s.
Use only the first 20 seconds, not the total time. Rate = 22 ÷ 20 = 1.1 cm³/s.

silver.display: Use the graph. Calculate the mean rate of reaction between 10 s and 30 s.

misconceptions.message: At 10 s volume = 12 cm³, at 30 s volume = 30 cm³. Rate = (30 − 12) ÷ (30 − 10) = 18 ÷ 20 = 0.9 cm³/s.
Use the CHANGE in volume (30 − 12 = 18 cm³), not the value at 30 s.

silver.display: 7.3 g of hydrochloric acid is dissolved in 250 cm³ of water. Calculate the concentration in g/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Convert cm³ to dm³ first: 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.25 dm³. Then 7.3 ÷ 0.25 = 29.2 g/dm³.
250 cm³ is NOT the same as 250 dm³. Divide by 1000: 250 cm³ = 0.25 dm³.

silver.display: 5.85 g of sodium chloride is dissolved in 500 cm³ of water. Calculate the concentration in g/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Convert: 500 cm³ = 0.5 dm³. Concentration = 5.85 ÷ 0.5 = 11.7 g/dm³.
500 cm³ = 0.5 dm³. Don't forget to convert before dividing.

silver.display: Use the graph. Calculate the mean rate of mass loss over the first 40 seconds.

misconceptions.message: At 40 s, mass loss = 0.28 g. Rate = 0.28 ÷ 40 = 0.007 g/s.

silver.display: Use the graph. At what time does the reaction finish? (When the graph becomes flat.)
silver.equation_hint: \(\text{reaction finishes when the line goes flat}\)

misconceptions.message: The mass loss stops increasing between 100 s and 120 s (both read 0.48 g). The reaction finishes at about 100 s.

worked_examples.question: A reaction produces 48 cm³ of gas in 60 seconds. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.

steps.label: Step 1 — Read from the graph
steps.content: At t = 0 s, volume = 0 cm³. At t = 20 s, volume = 22 cm³.

worked_examples.question: The graph below shows the volume of gas produced over time. Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 20 seconds.
7.3 g of hydrochloric acid is dissolved in 250 cm³ of water. Calculate the concentration in g/dm³.

steps: Identify what you need to find: magnification, image size, or actual size
Check units — convert both sizes to the same unit before calculating
Use ×1000 going smaller (mm→μm→nm) or ÷1000 going larger (nm→μm→mm)
Substitute into the magnification equation and calculate
State your answer with the correct unit (magnification has no unit)
method_card.title: Magnification and Unit Conversions
method_card.content:
Magnification questions always involve three quantities — magnification, image size and actual size. You'll be given two and asked to find the third.

Approach:

  1. Identify which quantity you need to find
  2. Check the units — both sizes must be in the same unit before you divide
  3. Convert if needed: multiply by 1000 going smaller (mm → μm → nm), divide by 1000 going larger
  4. Substitute and calculate
  5. If asked for actual size, rearrange: actual size = image size ÷ magnification

Common pitfalls:

  • Forgetting to convert units before dividing — if image is in mm and real size is in μm, convert one first
  • Dividing the wrong way round — magnification = image ÷ actual, NOT actual ÷ image
  • Leaving magnification with a unit — magnification has no unit
  • Standard form errors — count your zeros carefully for very small cell sizes

exam_context.frequency: Very common — appears regularly and links to Required Practical 1 (microscopy)

gold.display: A ribosome has a diameter of 25 nm. Express this in metres, giving your answer in standard form.

misconceptions.message: 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m. So 25 nm = 25 × 10⁻⁹ m = 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ m. Adjust to correct standard form.
nm to m: 25 nm = 25 × 10⁻⁹ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ m. Don't confuse nm (10⁻⁹) with μm (10⁻⁶).

gold.display: An electron micrograph shows a mitochondrion at ×40,000 magnification. The image is 80 mm long. Calculate the actual length in μm.

misconceptions.message: Actual = image ÷ magnification. Convert: 80 mm = 80,000 μm. Then 80,000 ÷ 40,000 = 2 μm.
You must convert mm to μm before dividing: 80 mm = 80,000 μm. 80,000 ÷ 40,000 = 2 μm.

gold.display: A white blood cell has an actual diameter of 12 μm. A red blood cell has an actual diameter of 7 μm. How many times wider is the white blood cell than the red blood cell? Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: Divide the larger by the smaller: 12 ÷ 7 = 1.714… ≈ 1.7 times wider.
The question asks how many times wider, so divide (12 ÷ 7 ≈ 1.7), don't subtract (12 − 7 = 5).

gold.display: A student measures an image of a cell as 45 mm. The actual cell is 0.015 mm. Calculate the magnification, then determine if this cell is likely to be a bacterium (1–5 μm), an animal cell (10–30 μm), or a plant cell (10–100 μm).

misconceptions.message: Magnification = 45 ÷ 0.015 = 3000. Actual size = 0.015 mm = 15 μm. This fits 10–30 μm = animal cell.
0.015 mm = 15 μm (multiply by 1000). 15 μm fits the range of an animal cell (10–30 μm).

gold.display: A virus is 300 nm in diameter. An electron microscope produces an image 18 mm across. Calculate the magnification.

misconceptions.message: Convert image: 18 mm = 18,000 μm = 18,000,000 nm. Magnification = 18,000,000 ÷ 300 = ×60,000.

gold.display: A student measures the image of a bacterial cell as 14 mm under ×4000 magnification. Another student measures the image of a plant cell as 48 mm under ×800 magnification. Which cell has the larger actual size, and by how many μm?

misconceptions.message: Bacterium: 14 mm = 14,000 μm, actual = 14,000 ÷ 4000 = 3.5 μm. Plant: 48 mm = 48,000 μm, actual = 48,000 ÷ 800 = 60 μm. Difference = 60 − 3.5 = 56.5 μm.
Don't compare image sizes — compare actual sizes. A larger image doesn't mean a larger cell if the magnification is higher.

bronze.display: A plant cell has an actual size of 100 μm. Under a microscope the image is 40 mm long. Calculate the magnification. (Convert the image to μm first.)

misconceptions.message: Convert the image to μm first: 40 mm = 40,000 μm. Then 40,000 ÷ 100 = ×400.
Magnification = image ÷ actual, not actual ÷ image. 40,000 ÷ 100 = 400.

bronze.display: Convert 0.5 mm to μm.

misconceptions.message: Going from mm to μm means going smaller, so multiply by 1000. 0.5 × 1000 = 500 μm.

bronze.display: A cheek cell is 60 μm across. An image of it is 12 mm across. What is the magnification?

misconceptions.message: Convert image to μm: 12 mm = 12,000 μm. Magnification = 12,000 ÷ 60 = ×200.
Magnification = image ÷ actual = 12,000 ÷ 60 = 200, not 60 ÷ 12,000.

bronze.display: Convert 7500 μm to mm.

misconceptions.message: Going from μm to mm means going larger, so divide by 1000. 7500 ÷ 1000 = 7.5 mm.

bronze.display: A microscope has a magnification of ×400. The image of a cell is 20 mm long. What is the actual size of the cell in μm?

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: actual = image ÷ magnification. Convert: 20 mm = 20,000 μm. Then 20,000 ÷ 400 = 50 μm.
Convert the image to μm before dividing: 20 mm = 20,000 μm. 20,000 ÷ 400 = 50 μm.

bronze.display: Convert 3 μm to nm.

misconceptions.message: Going from μm to nm means going smaller, so multiply by 1000. 3 × 1000 = 3000 nm.

bronze.display: An onion cell has an actual width of 80 μm. A student draws it 24 mm wide. Calculate the magnification.

misconceptions.message: Convert: 24 mm = 24,000 μm. Magnification = 24,000 ÷ 80 = ×300.

bronze.display: Which of these is the correct unit conversion?

misconceptions.message: 1 mm = 1000 μm. Think: milli = 10⁻³, micro = 10⁻⁶, so there are 10³ = 1000 μm in 1 mm.

silver.display: A bacterium has an actual length of 2 μm. A photograph shows it as 15 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the photograph.

misconceptions.message: Convert: 15 mm = 15,000 μm. Magnification = 15,000 ÷ 2 = ×7500.
Magnification = image ÷ actual = 15,000 ÷ 2 = 7500. If you got 0.000133, you divided the wrong way.

silver.display: An image of a cell is 36 mm long. The magnification used was ×1200. Calculate the actual size of the cell in μm.

misconceptions.message: Actual = image ÷ magnification. Convert: 36 mm = 36,000 μm. Then 36,000 ÷ 1200 = 30 μm.
Convert image to μm first: 36 mm = 36,000 μm. Then 36,000 ÷ 1200 = 30 μm.

silver.display: A red blood cell has a diameter of 7 μm. A student wants to draw it with a magnification of ×2000. How long should the drawing be, in mm?

misconceptions.message: Image = magnification × actual = 2000 × 7 = 14,000 μm = 14 mm.
Image size = 2000 × 7 = 14,000 μm. Convert to mm: 14,000 ÷ 1000 = 14 mm.

silver.display: A micrograph shows a sperm cell head as 8 mm across at ×5000 magnification. Calculate the actual size of the sperm head in μm.

misconceptions.message: Actual = image ÷ magnification. Convert: 8 mm = 8000 μm. Then 8000 ÷ 5000 = 1.6 μm.

silver.display: An E. coli bacterium is 2 μm long. Express this length in metres, giving your answer in standard form.

misconceptions.message: 1 μm = 10⁻⁶ m. So 2 μm = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m. The exponent is −6, not −3 (that would be mm).

silver.display: A palisade cell is 0.035 mm long. Convert this to μm.

misconceptions.message: mm to μm: multiply by 1000. 0.035 × 1000 = 35 μm.
0.035 × 1000 = 35, not 3.5 or 350. Move the decimal point 3 places right.

worked_examples.question: A cell has an actual size of 50 μm. Under a microscope the image measures 25 mm. Calculate the magnification.
An image of a bacterium is 30 mm long under a magnification of ×10,000. Calculate the actual size of the bacterium in μm.

steps.label: Step 1 — Convert actual size to metres
Step 2 — This is already the actual size
steps.content: The question asks for the actual size in metres — we just convert the given 2 μm.

worked_examples.question: A mitochondrion has an actual length of 2 μm. A student draws it 60 mm long. Calculate the actual size in metres and give your answer in standard form.

steps: Write each parent's genotype (two alleles per parent)
Draw a 2×2 Punnett square grid with one parent's alleles across the top and the other down the side
Fill in the four boxes by combining row + column alleles
Count genotypes/phenotypes and express as a ratio, fraction, or percentage
Check: do the numbers add up to 4 offspring (or 100%)?
method_card.title: Punnett Squares and Genetic Probability
method_card.content:
Punnett squares show all the possible combinations of alleles that offspring can inherit from two parents.

Key terminology:

  • Dominant allele — shown with a capital letter (e.g. B) — always expressed if present
  • Recessive allele — shown with a lowercase letter (e.g. b) — only expressed when two copies are present (bb)
  • Homozygous — two identical alleles (BB or bb)
  • Heterozygous — two different alleles (Bb) — also called a carrier if the recessive allele causes a disorder

Approach:

  1. Write out each parent's genotype (two alleles each)
  2. Put one parent's alleles across the top and the other's down the side
  3. Fill in the four boxes by combining the row and column alleles
  4. Count the genotypes and phenotypes to give ratios or percentages

Common pitfalls:

  • Forgetting that Bb and bB are the same genotype — count them together
  • Confusing genotype (letters) with phenotype (physical characteristic)
  • Not reading whether the question asks for a ratio, fraction, or percentage
  • In sex-linked inheritance, the allele is carried on the X chromosome — males have only one copy

exam_context.frequency: Very common — Punnett squares appear on nearly every Paper 2

gold.display: A couple both have dimples (dominant trait, D). They have a child without dimples. What are the genotypes of both parents?

misconceptions.message: The child without dimples is dd, so inherited a d from each parent. Both parents show dimples (so have at least one D). Both must be Dd.
DD × DD can only produce DD children. DD × Dd cannot produce dd. Only Dd × Dd can give a dd child.

gold.display: Red flower colour (R) is incompletely dominant with white (W). Heterozygous (RW) produces pink flowers. If two pink flowers are crossed, what percentage of offspring will be pink?

misconceptions.message: RW × RW gives RR (red), RW (pink), RW (pink), WW (white). That's 2 pink out of 4 = 50%.
This is incomplete dominance — the heterozygote has a blend phenotype. RW × RW → 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.

gold.display: Colour blindness is sex-linked and recessive (carried on the X chromosome). A carrier mother (X^B X^b) and a normal father (X^B Y) have a son. What is the probability that the son is colour-blind?

misconceptions.message: Sons get their X from mum. Mum is X^B X^b, so 50% chance of passing X^b. A son with X^b Y is colour-blind. Probability = 50%.
The father's Y chromosome has no allele for this trait. The son's colour vision depends entirely on which X he gets from his mother.

gold.display: In a genetics experiment, 120 pea plants are produced from a monohybrid cross. 91 have round seeds and 29 have wrinkled seeds. What is the expected ratio, and does the actual data closely fit this ratio?
options: Expected 1:1 — no, the data does not fit
Expected 3:1 — no, 91:29 is too far from 90:30
Expected 1:3 — yes, the data fits well

misconceptions.message: 3:1 predicts 90 round : 30 wrinkled. Actual is 91:29. 91 ÷ 29 = 3.14:1, which is very close to 3:1.
Real data rarely matches predicted ratios exactly. 91:29 is close enough to 3:1 (predicted 90:30) to support the model.

gold.display: A man with blood type A (genotype I^A i) and a woman with blood type B (genotype I^B i) have children. What percentage of their children could have blood type O?

misconceptions.message: I^A i × I^B i gives: I^A I^B (AB), I^A i (A), I^B i (B), ii (O). One out of four = 25%.
I^A and I^B are codominant with each other, but both are dominant over i. Only ii gives type O blood.

gold.display: Two parents who are both heterozygous (Ff) for cystic fibrosis have 3 children, none of whom has the condition. What is the probability that their fourth child will have cystic fibrosis?

misconceptions.message: Each pregnancy is independent. Previous children don't affect the probability. Ff × Ff always gives a 1 in 4 (25%) chance of ff.
The previous 3 children being unaffected does NOT increase or decrease the chance for the fourth. It's still 25%.

bronze.display: In a cross between two heterozygous parents (Bb × Bb), what ratio of offspring genotypes would you expect?

misconceptions.message: Bb × Bb gives: BB, Bb, Bb, bb — that's 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb.

bronze.display: Tall pea plants (T) are dominant to short (t). If two heterozygous plants (Tt × Tt) are crossed, what fraction of offspring would you expect to be short?

misconceptions.message: Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt. Only tt is short = 1 out of 4 = 1/4.

bronze.display: What is the genotype of an organism that is homozygous dominant for a trait represented by the letter A?

misconceptions.message: Homozygous = two identical alleles. Dominant = capital letter. So homozygous dominant = AA.

bronze.display: A homozygous dominant parent (BB) is crossed with a homozygous recessive parent (bb). What percentage of offspring will be heterozygous (Bb)?

misconceptions.message: BB × bb: every box gives Bb. All 4 offspring are Bb = 100% heterozygous.

bronze.display: In a Bb × Bb cross, how many out of 4 offspring would you expect to show the dominant phenotype?

misconceptions.message: BB, Bb, Bb all show the dominant phenotype (the dominant allele is present). Only bb shows recessive. So 3 out of 4.

bronze.display: A parent with genotype Bb produces gametes. Which alleles can be in the gametes?

misconceptions.message: Each gamete gets one allele from each pair. A Bb parent produces gametes with either B or b, not both.

bronze.display: Two homozygous recessive parents (bb × bb) are crossed. What percentage of offspring will show the recessive phenotype?

misconceptions.message: bb × bb: every box gives bb. All offspring are homozygous recessive = 100%.

bronze.display: A Bb × Bb cross produces four offspring. What percentage of the offspring would you expect to be homozygous (either BB or bb)?

misconceptions.message: Both BB and bb are homozygous. From Bb × Bb: 1 BB + 2 Bb + 1 bb. Homozygous = BB + bb = 2 out of 4 = 50%.
Homozygous means two identical alleles — both BB and bb count. 1 BB + 1 bb = 2 out of 4 = 50%.

silver.display: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). Two parents who are both carriers (Ff) have a child. What is the percentage chance that the child is a carrier but does NOT have cystic fibrosis?

misconceptions.message: Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff, ff. Carriers (Ff) = 2 out of 4 = 50%. Don't include ff (affected) or FF (not a carrier).

silver.display: In a cross Bb × bb, what percentage of offspring would you expect to show the recessive phenotype?

misconceptions.message: Bb × bb gives Bb, Bb, bb, bb. That's 2 dominant : 2 recessive = 50% recessive.

silver.display: Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele (D). A father with polydactyly (Dd) and an unaffected mother (dd) have children. What is the probability of a child having polydactyly?

misconceptions.message: Dd × dd gives Dd, Dd, dd, dd. Two have polydactyly (Dd) = 2 out of 4 = 50% = 1 in 2.

silver.display: If 200 offspring are produced from a Bb × Bb cross, how many would you expect to be homozygous recessive?

misconceptions.message: Bb × Bb gives 1/4 homozygous recessive (bb). 1/4 of 200 = 50 offspring.
The fraction that are bb is 1/4, not 1/2. 200 × 1/4 = 50.

silver.display: Tongue rolling (R) is dominant to non-rolling (r). A roller (Rr) and a non-roller (rr) have 80 children. How many would you expect to be non-rollers?

misconceptions.message: Rr × rr gives Rr, Rr, rr, rr. That's 2 out of 4 = 50% non-rollers. 50% of 80 = 40.

silver.display: Sickle cell trait is caused by allele Hb^S. A carrier (Hb^A Hb^S) and an unaffected person (Hb^A Hb^A) have children. What percentage could be carriers?

misconceptions.message: Hb^A Hb^S × Hb^A Hb^A gives: Hb^A Hb^A, Hb^A Hb^A, Hb^A Hb^S, Hb^A Hb^S. Two are carriers = 50%.

steps.label: Step 2 — Count phenotypes
steps.content:
BB = brown, Bb = brown (dominant), Bb = brown, bb = white

3 brown : 1 white

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: 25% would have white fur (1 out of 4)

worked_examples.question: Two heterozygous parents (Bb × Bb) are crossed. Brown fur (B) is dominant to white fur (b). What percentage of offspring would you expect to have white fur?

steps.label: Step 2 — Identify affected offspring
steps.content: Only ff has cystic fibrosis (homozygous recessive). That's 1 out of 4 boxes.

worked_examples.question: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). Two carrier parents (Ff × Ff) have a child. What is the probability that the child will have cystic fibrosis?

steps.label: Step 1 — Work backwards from the offspring
steps.content: One child has blue eyes (bb). This means the child must have inherited one b from each parent.

steps.label: Step 2 — Determine parent genotypes
steps.content: Both parents must carry at least one b allele. Since both parents have brown eyes (dominant phenotype), they must each also carry one B allele.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Both parents are Bb (heterozygous). This gives a 3:1 ratio, matching 3 brown : 1 blue.

worked_examples.question: A couple has four children. Three have brown eyes and one has blue eyes. Blue eyes are recessive (bb). Determine the genotypes of both parents. Explain your reasoning.

steps: Read the question — are you finding a mean, percentage change, or population estimate?
For mean: add all values, then divide by how many there are (exclude anomalies if told to)
For % change: (new − original) ÷ original × 100
For population estimate: mean per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area)
Give your answer to the number of decimal places or significant figures asked for
method_card.title: Sampling, Mean and Percentage Change
method_card.content:
These three calculations come up across both Biology papers — in ecology, experiments, and data analysis questions.

Mean: Add all the values together and divide by how many values there are. Always check for anomalous results (outliers) — the question may tell you to exclude them.

Percentage change: Shows how much a value has increased or decreased compared to the original. A negative answer means a decrease.

Population estimate: Used in ecology with quadrats. Find the mean count per quadrat, then scale up to the full area.

Common pitfalls:

  • Dividing by the wrong number when calculating the mean — count the number of data values carefully
  • Using the new value instead of the original as the denominator in percentage change
  • Forgetting to exclude anomalous results when told to
  • Mixing up the area of the quadrat with the total area in population estimates

exam_context.frequency: Very common — mean and percentage change appear on almost every paper; sampling in ecology questions

gold.display: In 2020 a lake had an estimated population of 450 fish. By 2023, the estimated population was 585. Between 2023 and 2025, it fell to 468. Calculate the percentage change from 2020 to 2025.

misconceptions.message: The question asks for the overall change from 2020 to 2025. Original = 450, final = 468. (468 − 450) ÷ 450 × 100 = 18 ÷ 450 × 100 = 4%.
Don't add the two separate percentage changes — just compare 2020 to 2025 directly: (468 − 450) ÷ 450 × 100 = 4%.

gold.display: A student uses 0.5 m² quadrats to sample a 300 m² field. In 10 quadrats they find: 2, 4, 3, 1, 5, 3, 4, 2, 3, 3 dandelions. The same field is surveyed a month later with results: 5, 7, 6, 4, 8, 6, 5, 7, 6, 6. Calculate the percentage change in estimated population.

misconceptions.message: You could also skip scaling: the population ratio is the same as the mean ratio. Mean went from 3 to 6 = 100% increase. But you must still use the correct % change formula.

gold.display: A farmer tests two fertilisers. Crop A yield increased from 3.2 tonnes to 4.8 tonnes. Crop B yield increased from 2.5 tonnes to 4.0 tonnes. Which fertiliser gave the greater percentage increase?

misconceptions.message: A had a bigger absolute increase (1.6 vs 1.5 tonnes), but B had a bigger percentage increase (60% vs 50%). Always compare percentages, not raw numbers.

gold.display: A student places 15 quadrats (each 0.25 m²) randomly in a 750 m² field. The total number of clover plants found across all 15 quadrats is 90. Estimate the population of clover in the field.

misconceptions.message: Mean per quadrat = 90 ÷ 15 = 6. Quadrats in field = 750 ÷ 0.25 = 3000. Population = 6 × 3000 = 18,000.
Total area ÷ quadrat area = 750 ÷ 0.25 = 3000 (not 750 ÷ 15). Mean = 6. Population = 6 × 3000 = 18,000.

gold.display: A scientist measures antibody concentration (arbitrary units) at 0, 7, 14, and 21 days after vaccination: 0.2, 1.4, 3.8, 3.6. Calculate the percentage change between day 0 and day 14.

misconceptions.message: The question asks for the change to day 14 (3.8), not day 21 (3.6). (3.8 − 0.2) ÷ 0.2 × 100 = 1800%.

gold.display: A student suggests that using more quadrats would make their population estimate more reliable. A second student says using larger quadrats would be better. Explain which student is more likely to improve reliability and why.
options: Student 1 — more quadrats gives a more representative sample of the whole area
Student 2 — larger quadrats cover more ground so the data is better
Both are equally valid — either approach works

misconceptions.message: More quadrats (more samples) gives a more representative mean, which improves reliability. Larger quadrats change what you measure but don't necessarily improve the reliability of the overall estimate.
Random placement reduces bias, but increasing the number of quadrats improves reliability by making the mean more representative.

bronze.display: A student measures the height of 5 bean plants: 12 cm, 15 cm, 14 cm, 13 cm, 16 cm. Calculate the mean height.

misconceptions.message: Sum = 12 + 15 + 14 + 13 + 16 = 70. There are 5 values. Mean = 70 ÷ 5 = 14 cm.

bronze.display: A population of bacteria increases from 500 to 650. Calculate the percentage change.

misconceptions.message: Use the original value (500) as the denominator: (650 − 500) ÷ 500 × 100 = 150 ÷ 500 × 100 = 30%.
Don't forget to multiply by 100: 150 ÷ 500 = 0.3, then 0.3 × 100 = 30%.

bronze.display: Calculate the mean of these pulse rates (bpm): 68, 72, 74, 70, 66.

misconceptions.message: Sum = 68 + 72 + 74 + 70 + 66 = 350. There are 5 values. Mean = 350 ÷ 5 = 70 bpm.

bronze.display: The mass of a plant increases from 2.0 g to 2.8 g over 4 weeks. Calculate the percentage increase in mass.
Which of the following is an anomalous result in this data set: 12, 14, 13, 28, 15, 11?

misconceptions.message: Most values cluster around 11–15. The value 28 is far from the others — it's the anomaly.

bronze.display: A student counts daisies in 4 quadrats: 8, 5, 7, 4. Calculate the mean number of daisies per quadrat.

misconceptions.message: Sum = 8 + 5 + 7 + 4 = 24. There are 4 quadrats. Mean = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 per quadrat.

bronze.display: A woodland had 80 squirrels last year. This year there are 60. Calculate the percentage change.

misconceptions.message: The population decreased: (60 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100 = −20 ÷ 80 × 100 = −25%. The negative sign shows a decrease.
Always divide by the original value (80), not the new value (60). (60 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100 = −25%.

bronze.display: The number of dandelions counted in 6 quadrats was: 3, 5, 4, 6, 3, 3. Calculate the mean.

misconceptions.message: Sum = 3 + 5 + 4 + 6 + 3 + 3 = 24. There are 6 values. Mean = 24 ÷ 6 = 4.

silver.display: A student uses 0.25 m² quadrats in a field of 100 m². The mean number of clover plants per quadrat is 6. Estimate the total population of clover in the field.

misconceptions.message: Number of quadrats in field = 100 ÷ 0.25 = 400. Population = 6 × 400 = 2400.
Don't just multiply mean by total area. Divide total area by quadrat area first: 100 ÷ 0.25 = 400. Then 6 × 400 = 2400.

silver.display: A patient's blood glucose drops from 8.4 mmol/L to 5.6 mmol/L after insulin. Calculate the percentage decrease. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: Change = 5.6 − 8.4 = −2.8. Percentage = −2.8 ÷ 8.4 × 100 = −33.3%. The question asks for the decrease, so answer is 33.3%.
Divide by the original (8.4), not the new value (5.6). 2.8 ÷ 8.4 × 100 = 33.3%.

silver.display: Five students measured the length of an onion cell under a microscope: 0.12 mm, 0.14 mm, 0.11 mm, 0.38 mm, 0.13 mm. One result is anomalous. Calculate the mean excluding the anomalous result.

misconceptions.message: 0.38 mm is the anomaly — it's far from the others. Exclude it: (0.12 + 0.14 + 0.11 + 0.13) ÷ 4 = 0.50 ÷ 4 = 0.125 mm.
After excluding the anomaly, you have 4 values, not 5. Sum = 0.50, mean = 0.50 ÷ 4 = 0.125 mm.

silver.display: A student uses 1 m² quadrats in a meadow of 500 m². The number of plantain in 8 quadrats was: 3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 3, 5, 4. Estimate the total population in the meadow.

misconceptions.message: Quadrat area is 1 m², so total area ÷ quadrat area = 500 ÷ 1 = 500. Population = 4 × 500 = 2000.

silver.display: The heart rate of a runner increased from 72 bpm at rest to 162 bpm during exercise. Calculate the percentage increase.

misconceptions.message: A percentage increase can be over 100% — it just means the value more than doubled. 90 ÷ 72 × 100 = 125%.

silver.display: The enzyme amylase broke down 15 mg of starch in 5 minutes. At a higher temperature, it broke down 9 mg in the same time. Calculate the percentage decrease in starch breakdown.

misconceptions.message: Original = 15, new = 9. Change = 9 − 15 = −6. Percentage = −6 ÷ 15 × 100 = −40%. Decrease = 40%.
The question asks for percentage decrease, so give a positive number: 40%.

steps: Identify which equation to use: KE = ½mv², GPE = mgh, W = Fd, or P = E/t
For KE: square the speed first (v²), then multiply by ½ and by mass
For GPE: use vertical height only, and g = 10 N/kg at Earth's surface
For power: calculate energy transferred first (e.g. GPE gained), then divide by time
method_card.title: Kinetic Energy, GPE and Power
method_card.content:
Four equations cover the calculations in this lesson — the key skill is picking the right one.

Kinetic energy: \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\). Square the speed before multiplying — this is the most common arithmetic error. Doubling speed quadruples KE.

Gravitational potential energy: \(E_p = mgh\). Use vertical height, not distance along a slope. g = 10 N/kg.

Work done: \(W = Fd\). Energy transferred when a force moves an object. Distance must be in the direction of the force.

Power: \(P = E/t\). The rate of energy transfer in watts. A two-step method — find energy first, then divide by time.

Common pitfalls:

  • Not squaring speed in the KE equation — write v² as a separate step
  • Using total length instead of vertical height for GPE
  • Forgetting to find energy before applying the power equation

exam_context.frequency: High — energy calculations appear in nearly every physics paper

gold.display: A 800 kg rollercoaster car starts from rest at the top of a 45 m drop. Calculate its speed at the bottom, assuming no energy losses. (g = 10 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Don't forget to take the square root at the end: v = √900 = 30 m/s, not 900.

gold.display: A 1,200 kg car travels at 30 m/s. An emergency forces the driver to brake to rest. Calculate the kinetic energy that must be removed by the brakes. Then calculate the average braking force if the car stops in 50 m.

misconceptions.message: Use W = Fd rearranged to F = W/d. The work done by brakes equals the KE removed.

gold.display: A motor lifts a 120 kg load by 8 m in 6 s. Calculate the power output of the motor in watts. (g = 10 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: P = E ÷ t, not E × t.

gold.display: A 500 g ball is launched upwards with 90 J of kinetic energy. Assuming all KE converts to GPE, calculate the maximum height reached. (g = 10 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Convert mass to kg first: 500 g = 0.5 kg. GPE = KE = 90 J. h = E/(mg) = 90/(0.5 × 10) = 18 m.
Rearrange E_p = mgh to h = E_p/(mg). Use mass in kg.

bronze.display: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed first: v² = 3² = 9. Then E_k = 0.5 × 2 × 9 = 9 J.

steps: Identify the useful energy output and total energy input (or use power values)
Calculate efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input
Multiply by 100 to express as a percentage
Find wasted energy = total input − useful output
method_card.title: Efficiency and Energy Resources
method_card.content:
Efficiency is a ratio — it has no unit. It tells you what fraction of the input energy is transferred usefully.

Key equations:

  • Efficiency = useful energy transferred ÷ total energy transferred
  • Efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input (works because time cancels)
  • Wasted energy = total input − useful output

Common pitfalls:

  • Putting wasted energy in the numerator instead of useful energy
  • Writing units (J or W) after an efficiency answer — it is dimensionless
  • Confusing efficiency as a decimal (e.g. 0.36) with efficiency as a percentage (36%)

exam_context.frequency: High — efficiency appears in most physics papers

gold.display: A coal power station generates 800 MW of electrical power from a thermal input of 2,000 MW. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage. Calculate how much power is wasted in MW.
A device has efficiency 0.65. In 30 seconds it uses 1,500 J of input energy. Calculate the useful energy output in 30 seconds.

misconceptions.message: Useful energy = efficiency × input = 0.65 × 1,500 = 975 J.

gold.display: A gas boiler has efficiency 0.85. It needs to deliver 12,750 J of useful heat energy. Calculate the total energy input required.

misconceptions.message: Total = useful ÷ efficiency = 12,750 ÷ 0.85 = 15,000 J.

gold.display: A student tests two lamps. Lamp A: 40 W input, 8 W light output. Lamp B: 12 W input, 3 W light output. Which is more efficient? Enter the efficiency of Lamp A as a decimal.

misconceptions.message: Lamp A: 8/40 = 0.20. Lamp B: 3/12 = 0.25. Lamp B is more efficient (0.25 > 0.20).

bronze.display: A device uses 200 J of energy and produces 50 J of useful output. Calculate its efficiency as a decimal.

misconceptions.message: Use useful output (50 J) in the numerator, not wasted energy. Efficiency = 50 ÷ 200 = 0.25.

bronze.display: A light bulb takes in 60 J and transfers 12 J as light. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

misconceptions.message: Multiply the ratio by 100 to get a percentage: (12/60) × 100 = 20%.

bronze.display: A device has a total energy input of 500 J. Its useful output is 350 J. How much energy is wasted?
A motor has useful power output of 300 W and total power input of 400 W. Calculate its efficiency as a decimal.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = useful ÷ total = 300 ÷ 400 = 0.75.

bronze.display: An electric kettle has efficiency 0.92. If the total input power is 2,000 W, calculate the useful power output.
A car engine takes in 60,000 J and has an efficiency of 0.30. Calculate the useful energy output.

silver.display: A wind turbine has a power input of 8,000 W from the wind and a useful electrical power output of 2,800 W. Calculate its efficiency as a percentage.
A device has efficiency 0.45 and useful power output of 900 W. Calculate the total power input.
A light bulb has efficiency 0.15. It has a power input of 60 W. Calculate the rate at which energy is wasted.
silver.equation_hint: Wasted = total input − useful output. Useful = efficiency × total.

misconceptions.message: Useful = 0.15 × 60 = 9 W. Wasted = 60 − 9 = 51 W.

steps: For charge: Q = I × t (coulombs = amperes × seconds)
For Ohm's law: V = IR. Rearrange to find I = V/R or R = V/I
Series total resistance: R_total = R1 + R2 + … Current is the same everywhere
Parallel circuits: pd is the same across every branch; total resistance is less than the smallest
method_card.title: Circuit Calculations
method_card.content:
Three equations cover all circuit calculations in this lesson.

Q = It: charge (C) = current (A) × time (s).

V = IR: potential difference (V) = current (A) × resistance (Ω). Always write the rearrangement explicitly before substituting.

Series vs Parallel — the most tested distinction:

  • Series: same current everywhere; pd splits across components; R_total = sum of all resistances.
  • Parallel: same pd across every branch; current splits; total resistance is less than any single branch.

Memory aid: 'Series Shares Voltage; Parallel Passes current equally.'

Common pitfalls:

  • Mixing up the current and pd rules for series/parallel
  • Not rearranging V = IR before substituting numbers

exam_context.frequency: High — circuit calculations appear in most physics papers

gold.display: A 12 V battery drives a current of 0.2 A through a series circuit of three resistors (10 Ω, 20 Ω and R). Calculate R.
gold.question: A 12 V battery drives a current of 0.2 A through a series circuit of three resistors (10 Ω, 20 Ω and R). Calculate R.

misconceptions.message: R_total = V ÷ I = 60 Ω. Subtract known resistances: R = 60 − 30 = 30 Ω.

misconceptions.message: R_total = V/I = 6/0.03 = 200 Ω. Thermistor R = 200 − 100 = 100 Ω.
Total resistance = V/I = 200 Ω. Thermistor = total − fixed = 100 Ω.

steps: For power: use P = VI when you know voltage and current; use P = I²R when you know current and resistance
For energy bills: convert power to kW (divide watts by 1,000) and time to hours
Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (hours)
Cost = energy (kWh) × price per kWh
method_card.title: Electrical Power and Energy Bills
method_card.content:
Unit errors destroy marks in energy-bill calculations. Check at the start: power must be in kilowatts, time in hours.

Power equations:

  • \(P = VI\) — use when you have voltage and current
  • \(P = I^2R\) — use when you have current and resistance
  • \(E = QV\) — energy transferred by a charge

Energy bills:

  • Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (hours)
  • Cost (p) = energy (kWh) × price per kWh (p)
  • 1 kWh = 3,600,000 J

Common pitfalls:

  • Using watts instead of kilowatts
  • Using minutes or seconds instead of hours
  • Forgetting to square current in P = I²R

steps: Density: ρ = m/V. Keep units consistent (g and cm³, or kg and m³)
SHC: ΔE = mcΔθ. Always calculate the temperature CHANGE (final − initial), not the final temperature
Latent heat: E = mL. Check whether the question asks about fusion or vaporisation
During a change of state temperature stays constant — use E = mL not ΔE = mcΔθ
method_card.title: Density, Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat
method_card.content:
Three equations, three common pitfalls.

Density: ρ = m/V. Keep units consistent — do not mix kg with cm³.

SHC: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\). The Δθ is the change in temperature: Δθ = final − initial. Using the final temperature instead is the most common error.

Latent heat: E = mL. During any change of state, temperature is constant. The latent heat of vaporisation of water (2,260,000 J/kg) is roughly 7× larger than the latent heat of fusion (334,000 J/kg).

Common pitfalls:

  • Using final temperature instead of temperature change in ΔE = mcΔθ
  • Confusing latent heat of fusion with latent heat of vaporisation
  • Mixing g/cm³ with kg/m³ without converting

exam_context.frequency: Medium — typically 1–2 questions per paper

gold.display: A 1.5 kg sample of water is heated from 20 °C to 100 °C, then completely vaporised. Calculate the total energy required. (c water = 4,200 J/kg/°C; L vaporisation = 2,260,000 J/kg)

misconceptions.message: Use the latent heat of vaporisation (2,260,000 J/kg) for boiling, not fusion.

gold.display: A metal cube has a mass of 486 g and sides 3 cm long. Calculate the density of the metal in g/cm³.

misconceptions.message: Volume of cube = 3³ = 27 cm³. ρ = 486/27 = 18 g/cm³.
Volume = side³ = 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cm³. Then ρ = 486/27 = 18 g/cm³.

gold.display: A heater supplies 120,000 J to 4 kg of a liquid and raises its temperature by 25 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of the liquid.

steps: Weight: W = mg. Mass (kg) is not the same as weight (N); g = 10 N/kg on Earth
Work done: W = Fd. Distance must be in the direction of the force
Hooke's law: F = ke. Extension e must be in metres (not cm)
Elastic PE: E_e = ½ke². Extension is SQUARED — doubling extension quadruples stored energy
method_card.title: Forces, Work Done and Elasticity
method_card.content:
Four equations that are commonly mixed up — learn the right one for the right context.

Weight: W = mg. This is a force (N), not a mass (kg). Mass is constant; weight changes with gravitational field strength.

Work done: W = Fd. The distance must be in the direction of the force (J = N m).

Hooke's law: F = ke, where k is the spring constant (N/m) and e is extension (m). Only valid up to the limit of proportionality — beyond that, plastic deformation occurs.

Elastic PE: \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^2\). Extension is squared — just like KE.

Common pitfalls:

  • Confusing mass (kg) and weight (N)
  • Using extension in cm instead of m in F = ke and E_e = ½ke²
  • Forgetting to square extension in the elastic PE equation

method_card.title: Speed, Acceleration and Motion Graphs
method_card.content:
Two equations and two graph types cover this lesson.

Speed: average speed (m/s) = distance (m) ÷ time (s).

Acceleration: a (m/s²) = change in speed (m/s) ÷ time (s). A negative value means deceleration.

Distance-time graph: gradient = speed. Steeper = faster. Horizontal = stationary.

Velocity-time graph: gradient = acceleration. Area under line = distance.

Common pitfalls:

  • Using final speed instead of change in speed for acceleration
  • Confusing the two graph types — a horizontal line means different things on each
  • Not using the correct area formula for the shape (triangle = ½ × base × height)

steps: Resultant force: F = ma (N = kg × m/s²). Rearrange to find a = F/m or m = F/a
Momentum (HT): p = mv (kg m/s). Conservation: total momentum before = total momentum after
Force from momentum change (HT): F = Δp ÷ Δt. Longer time = smaller force
Wave speed: v = f × λ. Rearrange to f = v/λ or λ = v/f
method_card.title: Newton's Laws, Momentum and Waves
method_card.content:
This lesson covers three equation families linked by Newton's laws.

F = ma: the resultant force equals mass × acceleration. If the resultant force is zero (Newton's first law), the object stays at rest or moves at constant speed.

Momentum (higher tier): p = mv (kg m/s). Momentum is conserved in a closed system. F = Δp/Δt — a longer collision time reduces peak force for the same change in momentum.

Wave speed: v = fλ. Units: m/s = Hz × m. All electromagnetic waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum.

Common pitfalls:

  • Not converting wavelength to metres before substituting into v = fλ
  • Confusing Newton's first law (zero resultant → constant speed) with Newton's second law (non-zero resultant → acceleration)

exam_context.frequency: High — F = ma and wave speed appear in most papers

Conservation of mass: in a closed system, total mass of reactants = total mass of products
method_card.title: Relative Formula Mass and Moles
method_card.content:
The mole is the 'bridge' between masses you can weigh and atoms you cannot see.

Mr calculation: List each element, multiply Ar by subscript, add up. H₂SO₄: (2×1) + 32 + (4×16) = 98.

Moles: moles = mass ÷ Mr. One mole has a mass in grams equal to Mr. One mole contains 6.0 × 10²³ particles.

Percentage by mass: (Ar × number of atoms ÷ Mr) × 100. Do not forget to multiply by 100.

Common pitfalls:

  • Not multiplying Ar by the subscript (e.g. treating H₂O as H + O instead of 2H + O)
  • Forgetting × 100 in the percentage calculation
  • Confusing open and closed systems when discussing mass changes

steps: Balance equations by changing coefficients only — never change formulae
Read off the mole ratio from the balanced equation coefficients
Convert given mass to moles: moles = mass ÷ Mr
Scale moles using the ratio, then convert back: mass = moles × Mr
method_card.title: Balancing Equations and Reacting Masses
method_card.content:
Reacting mass calculations always follow the same five steps.

Step 1: Write and balance the equation.

Step 2: Identify the mole ratio of the two substances you need.

Step 3: Convert the known mass to moles: moles = mass ÷ Mr.

Step 4: Use the ratio to find moles of the unknown.

Step 5: Convert back to mass: mass = moles × Mr.

Show all five steps clearly — method marks are available even if the final arithmetic is wrong.

Common pitfalls:

  • Changing a subscript instead of a coefficient when balancing
  • Skipping the mole ratio step
  • Basing calculations on the wrong reactant when a limiting reactant is specified

exam_context.frequency: High — reacting mass questions appear in most chemistry papers

steps: List all bonds broken in reactants — multiply each bond energy by the number of that bond type
List all bonds made in products — multiply each bond energy by the number of that bond type
ΔH = energy to break bonds − energy released making bonds
Negative ΔH = exothermic; positive ΔH = endothermic
method_card.title: Bond Energy Calculations
method_card.content:
Every bond energy calculation has two sections: bonds broken and bonds made.

Bonds broken — always endothermic (energy in). List each bond type in the reactants and multiply by its count.

Bonds made — always exothermic (energy out). List each bond type in the products and multiply by its count. Remember to multiply by coefficients in the balanced equation.

Overall: ΔH = energy in − energy out. Negative = exothermic; positive = endothermic.

Common pitfalls:

  • Not counting all bonds — in 2H₂O there are 4 O-H bonds total (not 2)
  • Getting the sign wrong — bond breaking is energy IN, bond making is energy OUT
  • Using the wrong bond type (C=O double bond has higher energy than C-O single bond)

exam_context.frequency: Medium — bond energy questions appear regularly

gold.display: N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3. Bond energies: N≡N = 945, H-H = 436, N-H = 391 kJ/mol. Calculate ΔH.

misconceptions.message: Bonds broken: N≡N (945) + 3×H-H (1308) = 2253 kJ. Bonds made: 2×NH3 = 6 N-H bonds = 6×391 = 2346 kJ. ΔH = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ/mol.
2NH3 has 6 N-H bonds total (3 per molecule × 2 molecules).

gold.display: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. Bond energies: C-H = 412, O=O = 498, C=O = 743, O-H = 463 kJ/mol. Calculate ΔH.

misconceptions.message: Broken: 4×C-H (1648) + 2×O=O (996) = 2644. Made: 2×C=O (1486) + 4×O-H (1852) = wait: CO2 has 2 C=O bonds, 2×H2O has 4 O-H. Made = 2×743 + 4×463 = 1486+1852 = 3338. ΔH = 2644−3338 = −694. (Note: use values as given — answer depends on bond energies provided to the student.)
Bonds broken: CH4 has 4 C-H bonds. Each O2 has 1 O=O. Count all bonds carefully.

gold.display: A reaction has bonds broken = 1,200 kJ and ΔH = +300 kJ/mol. Calculate the energy released when bonds form in the products.

misconceptions.message: ΔH = energy in − energy out. 300 = 1200 − energy out. Energy out = 1200 − 300 = 900 kJ.

misconceptions.message: Bonds broken: H-H (436) + Cl-Cl (243) = 679 kJ.

bronze.display: H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. Bond energies: H-Cl = 432 kJ/mol. What is the total energy released making all bonds in the products (2 HCl molecules)?

misconceptions.message: 2 HCl molecules = 2 H-Cl bonds: 2 × 432 = 864 kJ.

misconceptions.message: ΔH = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ/mol. The negative sign means exothermic.

misconceptions.message: Positive ΔH means more energy was absorbed breaking bonds than released making bonds — endothermic.

silver.display: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Bond energies: H-H = 436, O=O = 498, O-H = 463 kJ/mol. Calculate the total energy to break all bonds in the reactants.

method_card.title: Rates of Reaction and Concentrations
method_card.content:
Two key calculations: rate from data and concentration of a solution.

Mean rate: quantity produced (or used) ÷ time. The gradient of a rate-of-reaction graph gives the instantaneous rate at any point.

Concentration:

  • g/dm³ = mass (g) ÷ volume (dm³)
  • mol/dm³ = moles ÷ volume (dm³)
  • 1 dm³ = 1,000 cm³ — always convert before substituting

Common pitfalls:

  • Not converting cm³ to dm³ — the most common error in concentration calculations
  • Reading 'mean rate' from a specific point instead of total quantity ÷ total time
  • Confusing gradient (instantaneous rate) with overall mean rate

To find image size: image = actual size × magnification
Unit conversions: 1 mm = 1,000 µm; 1 µm = 1,000 nm. Multiply going to smaller units; divide going to larger.
method_card.title: Magnification and Unit Conversions
method_card.content:
The magnification formula has three forms — choose based on what you need to find.

Key rules:

  • Always ensure image size and actual size are in the same units before dividing
  • Magnification has NO units — it is a pure ratio
  • To go from mm → µm: multiply by 1,000. To go from µm → mm: divide by 1,000

Size reference points:

  • Plant cell: 10–100 µm
  • Animal cell: 10–30 µm
  • Mitochondrion: 1–10 µm
  • Bacterium: 1–10 µm
  • Virus: 20–300 nm

Common pitfalls:

  • Using different units for image and actual size (e.g. one in mm and the other in µm)
  • Forgetting to take the final unit conversion step
  • Multiplying by magnification instead of dividing when finding actual size

steps: Write parental genotypes and identify the gametes each parent can produce
Draw the 2×2 Punnett square, placing gametes along the top and left side
Fill in the four cells by combining one allele from each parent
Count outcomes: genotype ratio (TT:Tt:tt) then phenotype ratio (dominant:recessive). Express probability as fraction, decimal or %
method_card.title: Punnett Squares and Genetic Probability
method_card.content:
Punnett squares predict the probability of each offspring genotype — they do not guarantee specific numbers.

Key rules:

  • Capital letter = dominant (shown in BB or Bb)
  • Lower-case letter = recessive (only shown in bb)
  • A Tt × Tt cross always gives 3 dominant : 1 recessive phenotype ratio
  • A Bb × bb cross always gives 1:1 dominant : recessive phenotype ratio

Probability from a Punnett square: count how many of the 4 cells show each outcome. If 2 out of 4 cells show Bb, the probability is 2/4 = 0.5 = 50%.

Common pitfalls:

  • Confusing genotype ratio (TT:Tt:tt = 1:2:1) with phenotype ratio (3:1)
  • Stating '1 in 3' instead of '1 in 4' — always count all 4 cells

Example structure:

Standard 2×2 Punnett square: Aa × Aa
Aa
AAAAa
aAaaa

exam_context.frequency: High — genetics appears in most biology papers

gold.display: A plant with genotype TT is crossed with a plant of unknown genotype that shows the tall (dominant) phenotype. Two offspring show the short (recessive) phenotype. What must the unknown parent's genotype be? Enter 1 for TT, 2 for Tt, or 3 for tt.
gold.question:
Use a Punnett square to test each possibility — the cross that produces tt offspring identifies the unknown parent.

A plant with genotype Tt is crossed with a plant of unknown genotype that shows the tall (dominant) phenotype. Two of the offspring show the short (recessive) phenotype. What must the unknown parent's genotype be? Enter 1 for TT, 2 for Tt, or 3 for tt.

misconceptions.message: If TT × TT, no short offspring are possible. If TT × Tt: Tt and TT offspring only (all tall). But short offspring appeared, so unknown parent must be Tt (not TT). Wait — TT × Tt gives TT and Tt only (all tall). For short offspring to appear, we need a tt parent. Reconsider: TT × tt gives all Tt (all tall). Tt × Tt gives 25% tt. So if short offspring appeared, the mystery parent must be Tt and the cross is Tt × Tt. Answer: Tt = 2.
For recessive offspring (tt) to appear, both parents must carry the t allele. TT parent provides only T. The unknown parent must provide t, so must be Tt.
