steps: Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values
Estimated population = mean per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area)
Percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100
A positive result = increase; negative = decrease. Always divide by the ORIGINAL value
method_card.title: Sampling, Mean and Percentage Change
method_card.content:
Three calculations that appear regularly in ecology and data-handling questions.

Mean: add all values and divide by the count. Round sensibly — if data are whole numbers, one decimal place is usually fine.

Population estimate: mean per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area). Make sure you use the quadrat area (not just the number of quadrats).

Percentage change: % = (new − original) ÷ original × 100. Always use the original value in the denominator — using the new value is the most common error.

Common pitfalls:

  • Dividing by the new value instead of the original in percentage change
  • Not showing working for the mean (sum then divide)
  • Forgetting to account for quadrat size when estimating population

exam_context.frequency: Medium — data skills questions appear in most biology papers

Mean = 40/8 = 5 plants per quadrat. Quadrat area = 0.5 m². Units in field = 400/0.5 = 800. Population = 5 × 800 = 4,000.

steps: Calculate Mᵣ by adding all Aᵣ values in the formula
Find moles: n = m ÷ Mᵣ (or n = c × V if given concentration and volume)
For reacting masses: apply the molar ratio from the balanced equation
Convert moles back to mass: m = n × Mᵣ
Check using conservation of mass: total reactant mass = total product mass
method_card.title: Mole Calculations
method_card.content:
The mole is the chemist's counting unit. One mole always contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (the Avogadro constant). Because atoms and molecules are too small to count directly, we weigh them instead.

Core equations — learn all three:

  • \(n = \dfrac{m}{M_r}\) — moles from mass and relative formula mass
  • \(n = c \times V\) — moles from concentration (mol/dm³) and volume (dm³)
  • \(M_r = \dfrac{m}{n}\) and \(m = n \times M_r\) — rearrangements of the first equation

Finding Mᵣ step by step: Write the formula, count each type of atom, multiply by the Aᵣ from the data sheet, add up. For Ca(OH)₂: 1×40 + 2×(16+1) = 74.

Reacting masses — five-step routine:

  1. Write (or check) the balanced equation
  2. Read the molar ratio from the coefficients
  3. Calculate moles of the known substance: n = m ÷ Mᵣ
  4. Scale using the ratio to get moles of the unknown
  5. Convert back to mass: m = n × Mᵣ

Volume unit rule: n = c × V only works when V is in dm³. Divide cm³ by 1000 first.

exam_context.frequency: Very high — mole calculations underpin almost every quantitative chemistry question

gold.display: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the mass of iron produced from 24 g of iron(III) oxide. (Mᵣ: Fe₂O₃ = 160, Aᵣ: Fe = 56)

misconceptions.message: One mole of Fe₂O₃ produces two moles of Fe. Double the moles.

gold.display: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃. What mass of AlCl₃ is produced from 5.4 g of aluminium? (Aᵣ: Al = 27, Cl = 35.5)

misconceptions.message: The ratio 2Al : 2AlCl₃ simplifies to 1:1, so moles of Al = moles of AlCl₃.

gold.display: A student dissolves 5.3 g of Na₂CO₃ to make 250 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³. (Aᵣ: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: 250 cm³ = 0.25 dm³. Divide by 1000 before using c = n ÷ V.

misconceptions.message: From the equation, 1 mol N₂ produces 2 mol NH₃. Double the moles of N₂.

misconceptions.message: Mᵣ = mass ÷ moles = 5.6 ÷ 0.25 = 22.4. This is close to the Aᵣ of nitrogen (14), but that’s for N, not N₂ (Mr = 28). Accept Mᵣ = 22.4.
Rearrange n = m ÷ Mᵣ to get Mᵣ = m ÷ n = 5.6 ÷ 0.25 = 22.4.

method_card.title: Concentration and Titration
method_card.content:
Concentration tells you how many moles (or grams) of solute are packed into every cubic decimetre of solution. There are two versions of the formula — pick the right one based on what the question gives you.

Recall equations:

  • \(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\) — concentration in mol/dm³ (moles per litre)
  • \(c_{g} = \dfrac{m}{V}\) — concentration in g/dm³ (grams per litre)
  • \(n = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{M_r}\) — convert mass to moles using relative formula mass

The critical unit rule: Volume must be in dm³. If the question gives cm³, divide by 1000 before using any concentration formula.

Titration four-step pattern:

  1. Find moles of the substance you know (concentration × volume in dm³)
  2. Use the balanced equation mole ratio to find moles of the substance you don't know
  3. Use those moles with the other volume to find concentration
  4. Check units — answer in mol/dm³ or g/dm³ depending on the question

Reading the burette: The end point is where the indicator permanently changes colour. Read the bottom of the meniscus. Titre = final reading − initial reading. Use the mean of concordant (within 0.10 cm³) titres — discard the rough titre.

exam_context.frequency: High — concentration and titration calculations appear in almost every Chemistry paper

steps: For % yield: calculate theoretical yield (moles of limiting reactant → mole ratio → mass of product using Mr)
Apply: % yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100
For atom economy: identify desired product and all products in the balanced equation

For limiting reactant: convert both reactant masses to moles; compare actual mole ratio to equation ratio
method_card.title: Yield and Atom Economy
method_card.content:
Two distinct calculations — easy to confuse, so know which question is being asked before you start.

Percentage yield compares what you actually got from a reaction to the maximum you could theoretically have made:

\[\% \text{ yield} = \dfrac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100\]

Theoretical yield is calculated from the limiting reactant using mole ratios and Mr values. Yield is always ≤ 100%.

Atom economy measures how much of the total mass of all reactants ends up in the desired product:

\[\% \text{ atom economy} = \dfrac{M_r \text{ of desired product}}{M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100\]

Note: this uses Mr values from the balanced equation — you do not need actual masses. A reaction with only one product has 100% atom economy. By-products reduce atom economy.

Limiting reactant: the reactant that runs out first determines how much product can form. Find it by comparing the mole ratio from the equation to the moles actually present — the one that is present in smaller proportion relative to its coefficient is the limiting reactant.

Why do industries care? High atom economy means less waste and lower costs. Low yield means inefficiency — reactions may be reversible, product may be lost during purification, or a side reaction may occur.

exam_context.marks: 3–5 per calculation; may be combined with an evaluation of industrial trade-offs
exam_context.frequency: High — yield and atom economy appear most years at Higher Tier; atom economy sometimes at Foundation

gold.display: Consider the industrial production of iron: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for Fe. (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16, C = 12)

misconceptions.message: 2 Fe = 2×56 = 112. 3 CO₂ = 3×44 = 132. Total products = 112 + 132 = 244. Atom economy = (112÷244)×100 = 45.9%. (Double-check you are using 2 moles of Fe and 3 moles of CO₂.)
Sum the Mr of ALL products using their coefficients: 2Fe (112) + 3CO₂ (132) = 244. Atom economy for Fe = (112÷244)×100 = 45.9%.

gold.display: 24.3 g of aluminium reacts with excess chlorine: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃. The student collects 80.1 g of AlCl₃. Calculate the percentage yield. (Ar: Al = 27, Cl = 35.5)

misconceptions.message: Al:AlCl₃ ratio from equation is 2:2 = 1:1. One mole of Al gives one mole of AlCl₃.

gold.display: A pharmaceutical reaction produces the desired drug (Mr = 250) as well as a by-product (Mr = 150). The equation shows they form in a 1:1 ratio. Calculate the atom economy for the drug.

misconceptions.message: Total Mr of products = 250 + 150 = 400. Atom economy = (250÷400)×100 = 62.5%.

gold.display: Which reactant is the limiting reactant when 6.0 g of Mg reacts with 8.0 g of O₂? The equation is: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)
options: Mg, because it has the smaller mass
O₂, because it has the smaller mass
Mg, because the moles available are less than required by the mole ratio
O₂, because there is excess after the reaction

misconceptions.message: n(Mg) = 6÷24 = 0.25 mol. n(O₂) = 8÷32 = 0.25 mol. Ratio needed: 2 Mg : 1 O₂. With 0.25 mol O₂ you need 0.50 mol Mg but only have 0.25 mol — Mg is limiting.
Compare actual moles to the equation ratio. 0.25 mol Mg needs 0.125 mol O₂ — there is excess O₂, so Mg is the limiting reactant.

The question asks for yield of H₂, not ZnCl₂. Mr H₂ = 2. Theoretical = 0.10×2 = 0.20 g. % yield = (0.14÷0.20)×100 = 70%.

silver.display: Consider: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the atom economy for CO₂ as the desired product. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, H = 1)

Sum ALL product Mr values with their coefficients: CO₂ (44) + 2×H₂O (36) = 80. Atom economy = (44÷80)×100 = 55%.

silver.display: Ethanol can be made by fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for ethanol (C₂H₅OH). (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Multiply each Mr by its coefficient in the balanced equation before summing.

In the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, the atom economy is 100%. Yet the yield is only around 15% per pass. Explain the difference between atom economy and percentage yield in one sentence.
options: Atom economy measures what fraction of reactant atoms end up in the desired product; yield measures how much product was actually obtained compared with the maximum possible
Atom economy and yield are the same thing measured differently
Yield measures wasted atoms; atom economy measures how fast the reaction goes
Atom economy is only relevant in industry; yield applies to school experiments

misconceptions.message: Atom economy is about the reaction equation (types of products). Yield is about what you actually collect compared with the theoretical maximum.

method_card.title: Forces, Acceleration and Motion Equations
method_card.content:
Three connected equation families — always identify which one the question is testing before substituting numbers.

Recall equations:

  • \(F = ma\) — force (N) = mass (kg) × acceleration (m/s²)
  • \(a = \Delta v \div \Delta t\) — acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time
  • \(W = mg\) — weight (N) = mass (kg) × gravitational field strength (N/kg)

Given on the equation sheet (Higher Tier only):

  • \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) — connects velocity, initial velocity, acceleration and distance
  • (Also on sheet: v = u + at and s = ut + ½at²)

Stopping distance: thinking distance + braking distance. Thinking distance depends on reaction time and speed. Braking distance depends on speed, road conditions and brakes. Examiner reports note students who say crumple zones “absorb force” or “act as a barrier” — the correct explanation is that crumple zones increase the time over which the force acts, reducing peak force on passengers (from F = ma, if time is longer, deceleration is smaller, so force is smaller).

Unit checks: force in N, mass in kg, acceleration in m/s², velocity in m/s, distance in m. Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6.

exam_context.marks: 2–5 per calculation; crumple zones / safety often 3–6 mark extended response
exam_context.frequency: Very high — forces and motion calculations appear on almost every Physics paper

u = 0 (dropped from rest). v² = u² + 2as = 0 + 2×9.8×20 = 392. v = 19.8 m/s.

gold.display: A cyclist and bicycle together have a mass of 75 kg. The cyclist accelerates at 2.0 m/s² against a resistive force of 30 N. What is the driving force from the cyclist's legs?

misconceptions.message: Net force = ma = 75×2.0 = 150 N. Driving force − resistive force = net force → driving = 150 + 30 = 180 N.
F = ma gives the resultant force. Driving force = resultant + resistance = 150 + 30 = 180 N.

gold.display: A car crashes into a wall. Without crumple zones it stops in 0.05 s. With crumple zones it stops in 0.15 s. The car and driver have a combined mass of 1500 kg and are travelling at 15 m/s. Calculate the force with and without crumple zones and find the ratio.

misconceptions.message: Without: a = 15÷0.05 = 300 m/s². F = 1500×300 = 450000 N. With: a = 15÷0.15 = 100 m/s². F = 150000 N. Ratio = 450000÷150000 = 3. Three times greater without crumple zones.
Use a = Δv÷Δt for each scenario, then F = ma. Compare the two forces.

gold.display: A 0.50 kg ball is thrown upward at 14 m/s. Using v² = u² + 2as (g = 9.8 m/s²), calculate the maximum height reached. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

misconceptions.message: At max height, v = 0. 0 = 14² + 2×(−9.8)×s → 0 = 196 − 19.6s → s = 10.0 m (2 s.f.). Acceleration due to gravity is negative (upward throw).

They act as a rigid barrier between the car and the engine
They increase the stopping time, reducing the deceleration and the force on passengers

misconceptions.message: Longer stopping time → smaller deceleration (a = Δv/Δt) → smaller force (F = ma). Crumple zones extend the collision time, not block the force.

bronze.display: A truck decelerates from 20 m/s to rest in 8.0 s. Calculate the deceleration.
bronze.question: A truck decelerates from 20 m/s to rest in 8.0 s. Calculate the deceleration.
bronze.equation_hint: \(a = \Delta v \div \Delta t\). The answer will be a deceleration — state it as positive.

misconceptions.message: Δv = 20 − 0 = 20 m/s. a = 20 ÷ 8.0 = 2.5 m/s² deceleration.

bronze.display: A force of 300 N acts on an object that accelerates at 6.0 m/s². Calculate the mass of the object.
bronze.question: A force of 300 N acts on an object that accelerates at 6.0 m/s². Calculate the mass of the object.

silver.display: A 70 kg sprinter accelerates from rest to 9.0 m/s in 3.0 s. Calculate the average resultant force.
silver.question: A 70 kg sprinter accelerates from rest to 9.0 m/s in 3.0 s. Calculate the average resultant force.
silver.equation_hint: First find acceleration using \(a = \Delta v \div t\), then \(F = ma\)

silver.display: A car travelling at 15 m/s applies a braking force of 4500 N. The car has a mass of 1500 kg. Calculate how long it takes to stop.
silver.question: A car travelling at 15 m/s applies a braking force of 4500 N. The car has a mass of 1500 kg. Calculate how long it takes to stop.
silver.equation_hint: First find deceleration: \(a = F \div m\), then rearrange \(a = \Delta v \div t\) to find \(t\)

silver.display: A driver takes 0.70 s to react before braking. The car is travelling at 20 m/s. Calculate the thinking distance.
silver.question: A driver takes 0.70 s to react before braking. The car is travelling at 20 m/s. Calculate the thinking distance.
silver.equation_hint: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time. Use \(s = vt\) (no acceleration during thinking phase).

misconceptions.message: During the thinking phase the car travels at constant speed. s = v × t = 20 × 0.70 = 14 m.

silver.display: A car has a thinking distance of 12 m and a braking distance of 36 m at a certain speed. What is its total stopping distance?
silver.equation_hint: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance

misconceptions.message: Stopping distance = 12 + 36 = 48 m.

silver.display: A rocket of mass 20 000 kg produces a thrust of 300 000 N. Its weight is 196 000 N. Calculate the resultant force and the initial acceleration upwards.
silver.question: A rocket of mass 20 000 kg produces a thrust of 300 000 N. Its weight is 196 000 N. Calculate the resultant force and the initial acceleration upwards.

misconceptions.message: Resultant force = thrust − weight = 300000 − 196000 = 104000 N. a = F÷m = 104000÷20000 = 5.2 m/s².
Subtract weight from thrust to find net upward force before applying F = ma.

silver.display: A vehicle travelling at 30 m/s decelerates at 5.0 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping? Use v² = u² + 2as.
silver.question: A vehicle travelling at 30 m/s decelerates at 5.0 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping? Use v² = u² + 2as.
silver.equation_hint: \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). Here v = 0, u = 30, a = −5.0. Rearrange to find s.

misconceptions.message: 0 = 30² + 2×(−5.0)×s → 0 = 900 − 10s → s = 90 m. Deceleration is negative.
Remember to square u: 30² = 900, not 30.

A cyclist accelerates from 2.0 m/s to 8.0 m/s in 4.0 s. The total mass of cyclist and bike is 80 kg. Calculate the resultant force.

steps: Identify the equation needed from the quantities given in the question
Check units: mass in kg, speed in m/s, height in m, energy in J, power in W
For KE: square the speed first, then multiply by ½ and mass
For efficiency: useful ÷ total (result between 0 and 1, or multiply by 100 for %)
State the answer with the correct unit
method_card.title: Energy, Power and Efficiency
method_card.content:
These are the most frequently tested physics calculations. Learn each equation and its rearrangements cold.

Recall equations (must memorise):

  • \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) — kinetic energy (J) = ½ × mass (kg) × speed² (m/s)²
  • \(E_p = mgh\) — gravitational PE (J) = mass (kg) × g (N/kg) × height (m)
  • \(P = \dfrac{E}{t}\) — power (W) = energy (J) ÷ time (s)
  • \(P = IV\) — electrical power (W) = current (A) × potential difference (V)
  • \(P = I^2R\) — power using resistance
  • \(\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{useful output energy}}{\text{total input energy}}\) — express as a decimal or percentage

Use g = 9.8 N/kg unless the question specifies otherwise.

Common errors:

  • For KE: always square the speed first, then multiply by ½ and mass. Forgetting to square is the most common single error in Physics exams.
  • Efficiency must be between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%). If you get above 1, you have divided the wrong way round.
  • For P = IV, current is in amperes and pd is in volts — check both before substituting.

exam_context.marks: 2–5 marks per calculation; efficiency may include a follow-up on energy wasted as heat
exam_context.frequency: Very high — energy and power calculations appear in virtually every Physics paper

gold.display: A 1500 kg car travelling at 25 m/s brakes to rest. All kinetic energy is converted to thermal energy in the brakes. Calculate the temperature rise of the 15 kg steel brake discs. (Specific heat capacity of steel = 500 J/kg°C)

misconceptions.message: KE = ½mv² = 0.5×1500×625 = 468750 J. Then use ΔE = mcΔθ rearranged: Δθ = ΔE÷(mc) = 468750÷7500 = 62.5°C.

gold.display: A generator produces 230 V and has an internal resistance of 2.0 Ω. If the current is 10 A, calculate (a) the electrical power output to the external circuit and (b) the power wasted internally.

misconceptions.message: Output power P = IV = 10 × 230 = 2300 W. Internal power = I²R = 10² × 2.0 = 200 W.
Output: P = IV = 2300 W. Internal waste: P = I²R = 100 × 2.0 = 200 W.

gold.display: A wind turbine produces 5.0 MW of electrical power. The wind supplies 12 MW to the blades. Calculate the efficiency and the power wasted.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = useful ÷ total = 5.0÷12 = 0.417. Power wasted = 12 − 5 = 7 MW.
Efficiency = 5.0÷12 = 0.417 (41.7%). Never exceed 1 (100%).

gold.display: A 70 kg person runs up a flight of stairs (vertical height 5.0 m) in 4.0 s. Calculate their useful power output. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Find GPE gained first (mgh), then divide by time to get power.

gold.display: A ball of mass 0.4 kg is dropped from a height of 20 m. It bounces back to 12 m. Calculate the energy lost on impact. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Calculate initial and final GPE separately, then subtract.

gold.display: A mains appliance (230 V) has a power rating of 1150 W. Calculate the current drawn and the resistance. Give resistance to 3 significant figures.

misconceptions.message: First I = P÷V = 5.0 A, then R = V÷I = 46.0 Ω.

bronze.display: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 1200 kg car travelling at 30 m/s.

misconceptions.message: v² = 30² = 900. Eₖ = 0.5 × 1200 × 900 = 540 000 J. Don't multiply by 30 without squaring first.
Remember the ½ in Eₖ = ½mv².

bronze.display: A 50 kg cyclist rides at 10 m/s. Calculate their kinetic energy.

misconceptions.message: Eₖ = ½ × 50 × 100 = 2500 J. The ½ halves the answer.

bronze.display: Calculate the gravitational PE of a 5.0 kg object raised 3.0 m above the ground. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Ep = 5.0 × 9.8 × 3.0 = 147 J. All three values must be multiplied together.

bronze.display: An electric heater transfers 9000 J of energy in 3 minutes. Calculate the power output in watts.
bronze.equation_hint: \(P = E \div t\). Convert minutes to seconds first.

misconceptions.message: 3 minutes = 180 s. P = 9000 ÷ 180 = 50 W. Always convert time to seconds.

bronze.display: A lamp operates at 12 V and draws a current of 2.5 A. Calculate its power.

misconceptions.message: P = IV = 2.5 × 12 = 30 W. Don't divide — multiply current by voltage.

bronze.display: A machine has an input of 5000 J and a useful output of 3500 J. Calculate the efficiency as a decimal.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = 3500 ÷ 5000 = 0.7. Don't divide input by output.
Efficiency is always useful ÷ total. The answer should be between 0 and 1.

bronze.display: A kettle has a power rating of 2000 W. How much energy does it transfer in 90 s?
bronze.equation_hint: Rearrange \(P = E \div t\) to find \(E = P \times t\)

bronze.display: A motor uses a current of 5 A at a potential difference of 240 V. Calculate its power.

silver.display: A 0.5 kg ball is thrown upward and reaches a height of 10 m above the release point. Calculate the increase in gravitational PE. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A 2.0 kg object slides down a frictionless slope and falls a vertical height of 5.0 m. Assuming all GPE converts to KE, calculate the speed at the bottom. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
silver.equation_hint: GPE lost = KE gained. Set \(mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\), masses cancel, rearrange for v.

misconceptions.message: mgh = ½mv² → v² = 2gh = 2×9.8×5 = 98 → v = √98 = 9.9 m/s. Remember to square-root.
v² = 2gh (the 2 comes from the ½ in ½mv²). v = √(2×9.8×5) = 9.9 m/s.

silver.display: An electric motor has an input power of 800 W and efficiency of 0.75. Calculate the useful power output.
silver.equation_hint: Rearrange efficiency formula: useful output = efficiency × total input

misconceptions.message: Useful output = efficiency × input = 0.75 × 800 = 600 W. Don't divide.

silver.display: A resistor with resistance 20 Ω carries a current of 3.0 A. Calculate the power dissipated.

misconceptions.message: P = I²R = 3.0² × 20 = 9 × 20 = 180 W. Square the current first.
Use P = I²R when you have current and resistance. P = 9 × 20 = 180 W.

silver.display: A car's engine provides 45 000 J of energy. Only 36 000 J does useful work. Calculate the percentage efficiency.
A phone charger draws 0.5 A at 5.0 V. How much energy does it transfer in 2 hours?
silver.equation_hint: First find power: \(P = IV\), then energy: \(E = Pt\) (convert hours to seconds).

misconceptions.message: Always convert hours to seconds: 2 hours = 7200 s.

steps.label: Step 1 — Calculate useful energy output (GPE gained)

steps: Wave equation: identify two of {v, f, λ} and solve for the third using v = fλ
Density: identify two of {ρ, m, V} and solve for the third using ρ = m ÷ V
Half-life: find n = total time ÷ half-life period, then halve the initial activity n times
For density problems, check unit consistency — convert cm³ to m³ if needed (÷ 1 000 000)
State the answer with the correct unit every time
method_card.title: Waves, Half-Life and Density
method_card.content:
Three distinct recall equations from different areas of physics — all appear every year and are straightforward once the equations are secure.

Recall equations:

  • \(v = f\lambda\) — wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m)
  • \(\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}\) — density (kg/m³) = mass (kg) ÷ volume (m³)

Half-life (exponential decay — no single formula needed for GCSE): After each half-life, the count rate (or number of undecayed nuclei) halves. Strategy: count how many half-lives fit in the given time, then halve repeatedly. For multi-step questions, construct a table:

Number of half-livesActivity remaining
0Initial
1½ of initial
2¼ of initial
3⅛ of initial

Unit checks:
Wave equation: wavelength in metres, frequency in Hz (= per second), speed in m/s. Density: mass in kg, volume in m³ (note: 1 cm³ = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m³; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³).

exam_context.marks: 2–4 marks per calculation; half-life may be paired with graph reading or context questions
exam_context.frequency: High — all three equation types appear regularly; half-life calculation is almost annual

gold.display: A radioactive source has an activity of 5400 Bq. After 60 minutes its activity is 675 Bq. Calculate the half-life in minutes.

misconceptions.message: 5400 → 2700 → 1350 → 675: 3 halvings. Half-life = 60 ÷ 3 = 20 minutes.
Count halvings from 5400 to 675: divide by 2 three times. 60 min ÷ 3 = 20 min.

gold.display: An ocean wave has a speed of 15 m/s and a period of 8.0 s. Calculate (a) the frequency and (b) the wavelength.
gold.question: An ocean wave has a speed of 15 m/s and a period of 8.0 s. Calculate (a) the frequency and (b) the wavelength.

misconceptions.message: First convert period to frequency: f = 1/T = 0.125 Hz. Then λ = v/f = 15/0.125 = 120 m.

gold.display: A hollow steel ball has an outer volume of 120 cm³ and a mass of 250 g. Calculate the density of the steel ball in g/cm³ and explain why this is less than the density of solid steel (≈7.8 g/cm³).
options: 2.1 g/cm³ — less than solid steel because part of the volume is air, not steel
7.8 g/cm³ — the density is the same because the material is the same
2.1 g/cm³ — less than solid steel because the ball is cooler
0.48 g/cm³ — calculated using total volume without accounting for the shell

misconceptions.message: ρ = 250÷120 = 2.08 g/cm³ ≈ 2.1 g/cm³. This is less than solid steel (7.8) because the total volume includes the hollow air space, not just steel.

gold.display: A gamma source decreases from 6400 counts/min to 50 counts/min in 96 minutes. Calculate the half-life. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: Count how many times you halve 6400 to reach 50: that is 7 times (6400→…→50). 7 half-lives fit in 96 min, so half-life = 96÷7 ≈ 13.7 min.

gold.display: An X-ray photon has a wavelength of 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the frequency. Give your answer as a coefficient × 10¹⁸ (enter the coefficient, e.g. 3.0).
gold.question: An X-ray photon has a wavelength of 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the frequency. Give your answer as a coefficient × 10¹⁸ (enter the coefficient, e.g. 3.0).

misconceptions.message: f = v÷λ. When dividing in standard form, subtract the exponent: 10⁸÷10⁻¹⁰ = 10¹⁸. f = 3.0×10¹⁸ Hz.

gold.display: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 6 hours. A hospital needs it to have at least 25% of its original activity when it arrives. The transit time is 12 hours. Is the sample still usable on arrival?
options: Yes — 12 hours is 2 half-lives, leaving 25% of original activity
No — 12 hours is 3 half-lives, leaving only 12.5% of original activity
Yes — activity does not decrease significantly over 12 hours
No — any radioactive decay makes the sample unusable

misconceptions.message: n = 12÷6 = 2 half-lives. ½ × ½ = ¼ = 25% of original. Just meets the 25% threshold — the sample is borderline usable.
2 half-lives → activity × (½)² = ¼ = 25%. Exactly 25% remains, just meeting the minimum.

bronze.display: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 6.8 m. Calculate the wave speed.
bronze.question: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 6.8 m. Calculate the wave speed.

misconceptions.message: v = f × λ = 50 × 6.8 = 340 m/s. Don't add frequency and wavelength.

bronze.display: A wave travels at 300 000 000 m/s with a wavelength of 0.10 m. Calculate the frequency.
bronze.question: A wave travels at 300 000 000 m/s with a wavelength of 0.10 m. Calculate the frequency.

misconceptions.message: f = v ÷ λ = 3×10⁸ ÷ 0.10 = 3×10⁹ Hz. Don't divide λ by v.

bronze.display: An object has a mass of 500 g and a volume of 250 cm³. Calculate the density in g/cm³.
bronze.equation_hint: \(\rho = m \div V\) — units match (g and cm³), so answer is in g/cm³.

misconceptions.message: ρ = 500 ÷ 250 = 2.0 g/cm³. Don't divide volume by mass.

bronze.display: A radioactive source has an initial count rate of 800 Bq. After one half-life, what is the count rate?
bronze.equation_hint: After one half-life, the activity halves.

misconceptions.message: After one half-life the count rate is halved: 800 ÷ 2 = 400 Bq.

bronze.display: A source has an activity of 320 Bq. Its half-life is 5 years. What is the activity after 15 years?
bronze.equation_hint: How many half-lives in 15 years? Then halve that many times.

bronze.display: A radio wave has a frequency of 100 MHz (1×10⁸ Hz) and travels at 3×10⁸ m/s. Calculate its wavelength.
bronze.question: A radio wave has a frequency of 100 MHz (1×10⁸ Hz) and travels at 3×10⁸ m/s. Calculate its wavelength.

bronze.display: A block of iron has mass 7.8 kg and volume 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Calculate the density in kg/m³.
A source has an initial count rate of 3200 Bq and a half-life of 10 minutes. What is the count rate after 40 minutes?

silver.display: The activity of a radioactive isotope falls from 1000 Bq to 125 Bq in 30 days. Calculate the half-life.
silver.equation_hint: How many times do you have to halve 1000 to reach 125? Then divide total time by that number.

misconceptions.message: 1000 → 500 → 250 → 125: that is 3 halvings. Half-life = 30 ÷ 3 = 10 days.
Count halvings: 1000÷2=500, ÷2=250, ÷2=125 — 3 half-lives. Half-life = 30÷3 = 10 days.

silver.display: An ultrasound pulse travels at 1500 m/s in soft tissue. The pulse has a wavelength of 0.15 mm. Calculate the frequency in Hz. (1 mm = 0.001 m)
silver.question: An ultrasound pulse travels at 1500 m/s in soft tissue. The pulse has a wavelength of 0.15 mm. Calculate the frequency in Hz. (1 mm = 0.001 m)
silver.equation_hint: Convert wavelength to metres first, then \(f = v \div \lambda\)

silver.display: A wooden block of density 0.80 g/cm³ has a volume of 500 cm³. Calculate its mass in grams.

misconceptions.message: m = ρ × V = 0.80 × 500 = 400 g. Units match (g/cm³ × cm³ = g).

silver.display: A sample of carbon-14 has a half-life of approximately 5700 years. A fossil bone has 25% of the original carbon-14 activity. Estimate the age of the fossil.

misconceptions.message: 25% = ¼ of original. 100% → 50% (1 half-life) → 25% (2 half-lives). Age = 2 × 5700 = 11400 years.
Halving twice gives ¼ of original. 2 half-lives × 5700 years = 11400 years.

silver.display: A stone has a mass of 1.62 kg. When placed in a measuring cylinder it displaces 600 cm³ of water. Calculate the density of the stone in kg/m³.
silver.equation_hint: Convert cm³ to m³ (÷ 1 000 000), then \(\rho = m \div V\)

misconceptions.message: 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³. Multiply cm³ by 10⁻⁶ to convert to m³.

silver.display: A seismic P-wave travels at 6000 m/s through rock. If it has a frequency of 0.5 Hz, calculate its wavelength.
silver.question: A seismic P-wave travels at 6000 m/s through rock. If it has a frequency of 0.5 Hz, calculate its wavelength.

misconceptions.message: λ = v ÷ f = 6000 ÷ 0.5 = 12000 m (12 km). Dividing by a number less than 1 gives a larger result.

steps: Identify which equation to use: KE = ½mv², GPE = mgh, W = Fd, or P = E/t
For KE: square the speed first (v²), then multiply by ½ and by mass
For GPE: use vertical height only, and g = 10 N/kg at Earth's surface
For power: calculate energy transferred first (e.g. GPE gained), then divide by time
method_card.title: Kinetic Energy, GPE and Power
method_card.content:
Four equations cover the calculations in this lesson — the key skill is picking the right one.

Kinetic energy: \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\). Square the speed before multiplying — this is the most common arithmetic error. Doubling speed quadruples KE.

Gravitational potential energy: \(E_p = mgh\). Use vertical height, not distance along a slope. g = 10 N/kg.

Work done: \(W = Fd\). Energy transferred when a force moves an object. Distance must be in the direction of the force.

Power: \(P = E/t\). The rate of energy transfer in watts. A two-step method — find energy first, then divide by time.

Common pitfalls:

  • Not squaring speed in the KE equation — write v² as a separate step
  • Using total length instead of vertical height for GPE
  • Forgetting to find energy before applying the power equation

exam_context.frequency: High — energy calculations appear in nearly every physics paper

gold.display: A 800 kg rollercoaster car starts from rest at the top of a 45 m drop. Calculate its speed at the bottom, assuming no energy losses. (g = 10 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Don't forget to take the square root at the end: v = √900 = 30 m/s, not 900.

gold.display: A 1,200 kg car travels at 30 m/s. An emergency forces the driver to brake to rest. Calculate the kinetic energy that must be removed by the brakes. Then calculate the average braking force if the car stops in 50 m.

misconceptions.message: Use W = Fd rearranged to F = W/d. The work done by brakes equals the KE removed.

gold.display: A motor lifts a 120 kg load by 8 m in 6 s. Calculate the power output of the motor in watts. (g = 10 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: P = E ÷ t, not E × t.

gold.display: A 500 g ball is launched upwards with 90 J of kinetic energy. Assuming all KE converts to GPE, calculate the maximum height reached. (g = 10 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Convert mass to kg first: 500 g = 0.5 kg. GPE = KE = 90 J. h = E/(mg) = 90/(0.5 × 10) = 18 m.
Rearrange E_p = mgh to h = E_p/(mg). Use mass in kg.

gold.display: A 60 kg person climbs stairs, gaining 3 m of vertical height in 4 s. Calculate the useful power output. (g = 10 N/kg)

bronze.display: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed first: v² = 3² = 9. Then E_k = 0.5 × 2 × 9 = 9 J.

bronze.display: A 5 kg object is lifted 4 m vertically. Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy. (g = 10 N/kg)
A force of 50 N moves an object 3 m in the direction of the force. Calculate the work done.
A device transfers 600 J of energy in 20 seconds. Calculate its power.

misconceptions.message: P = E ÷ t = 600 ÷ 20 = 30 W. Divide energy by time, not multiply.

bronze.display: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 10 kg skateboard moving at 4 m/s.
A 3 kg book falls from a shelf 2 m above the floor. Calculate the GPE it loses. (g = 10 N/kg)
An appliance uses 1,500 J in 5 seconds. What is its power?
A horizontal push of 30 N moves a box 5 m along a flat floor. Calculate the work done.

A 500 W motor lifts a load for 12 seconds. Calculate the energy transferred.

silver.equation_hint: GPE lost = KE gained. Rearrange \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) for v.

steps: Identify the useful energy output and total energy input (or use power values)
Calculate efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input
Multiply by 100 to express as a percentage
Find wasted energy = total input − useful output
method_card.title: Efficiency and Energy Resources
method_card.content:
Efficiency is a ratio — it has no unit. It tells you what fraction of the input energy is transferred usefully.

Key equations:

  • Efficiency = useful energy transferred ÷ total energy transferred
  • Efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input (works because time cancels)
  • Wasted energy = total input − useful output

Common pitfalls:

  • Putting wasted energy in the numerator instead of useful energy
  • Writing units (J or W) after an efficiency answer — it is dimensionless
  • Confusing efficiency as a decimal (e.g. 0.36) with efficiency as a percentage (36%)

exam_context.frequency: High — efficiency appears in most physics papers

gold.display: A coal power station generates 800 MW of electrical power from a thermal input of 2,000 MW. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage. Calculate how much power is wasted in MW.
A device has efficiency 0.65. In 30 seconds it uses 1,500 J of input energy. Calculate the useful energy output in 30 seconds.

misconceptions.message: Useful energy = efficiency × input = 0.65 × 1,500 = 975 J.

gold.display: A gas boiler has efficiency 0.85. It needs to deliver 12,750 J of useful heat energy. Calculate the total energy input required.

misconceptions.message: Total = useful ÷ efficiency = 12,750 ÷ 0.85 = 15,000 J.

gold.display: A student tests two lamps. Lamp A: 40 W input, 8 W light output. Lamp B: 12 W input, 3 W light output. Which is more efficient? Enter the efficiency of Lamp A as a decimal.

misconceptions.message: Lamp A: 8/40 = 0.20. Lamp B: 3/12 = 0.25. Lamp B is more efficient (0.25 > 0.20).

bronze.display: A device uses 200 J of energy and produces 50 J of useful output. Calculate its efficiency as a decimal.

misconceptions.message: Use useful output (50 J) in the numerator, not wasted energy. Efficiency = 50 ÷ 200 = 0.25.

bronze.display: A light bulb takes in 60 J and transfers 12 J as light. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

misconceptions.message: Multiply the ratio by 100 to get a percentage: (12/60) × 100 = 20%.

bronze.display: A device has a total energy input of 500 J. Its useful output is 350 J. How much energy is wasted?

method_card.title: Circuit Calculations
method_card.content:
Three equations cover all circuit calculations in this lesson.

Q = It: charge (C) = current (A) × time (s).

V = IR: potential difference (V) = current (A) × resistance (Ω). Always write the rearrangement explicitly before substituting.

Series vs Parallel — the most tested distinction:

  • Series: same current everywhere; pd splits across components; R_total = sum of all resistances.
  • Parallel: same pd across every branch; current splits; total resistance is less than any single branch.

Memory aid: 'Series Shares Voltage; Parallel Passes current equally.'

Common pitfalls:

  • Mixing up the current and pd rules for series/parallel
  • Not rearranging V = IR before substituting numbers

method_card.title: Electrical Power and Energy Bills
method_card.content:
Unit errors destroy marks in energy-bill calculations. Check at the start: power must be in kilowatts, time in hours.

Power equations:

  • \(P = VI\) — use when you have voltage and current
  • \(P = I^2R\) — use when you have current and resistance
  • \(E = QV\) — energy transferred by a charge

Energy bills:

  • Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (hours)
  • Cost (p) = energy (kWh) × price per kWh (p)
  • 1 kWh = 3,600,000 J

Common pitfalls:

  • Using watts instead of kilowatts
  • Using minutes or seconds instead of hours
  • Forgetting to square current in P = I²R

steps: Density: ρ = m/V. Keep units consistent (g and cm³, or kg and m³)
SHC: ΔE = mcΔθ. Always calculate the temperature CHANGE (final − initial), not the final temperature
Latent heat: E = mL. Check whether the question asks about fusion or vaporisation
During a change of state temperature stays constant — use E = mL not ΔE = mcΔθ
method_card.title: Density, Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat
method_card.content:
Three equations, three common pitfalls.

Density: ρ = m/V. Keep units consistent — do not mix kg with cm³.

SHC: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\). The Δθ is the change in temperature: Δθ = final − initial. Using the final temperature instead is the most common error.

Latent heat: E = mL. During any change of state, temperature is constant. The latent heat of vaporisation of water (2,260,000 J/kg) is roughly 7× larger than the latent heat of fusion (334,000 J/kg).

Common pitfalls:

  • Using final temperature instead of temperature change in ΔE = mcΔθ
  • Confusing latent heat of fusion with latent heat of vaporisation
  • Mixing g/cm³ with kg/m³ without converting

steps: Weight: W = mg. Mass (kg) is not the same as weight (N); g = 10 N/kg on Earth
Work done: W = Fd. Distance must be in the direction of the force
Hooke's law: F = ke. Extension e must be in metres (not cm)
Elastic PE: E_e = ½ke². Extension is SQUARED — doubling extension quadruples stored energy
method_card.title: Forces, Work Done and Elasticity
method_card.content:
Four equations that are commonly mixed up — learn the right one for the right context.

Weight: W = mg. This is a force (N), not a mass (kg). Mass is constant; weight changes with gravitational field strength.

Work done: W = Fd. The distance must be in the direction of the force (J = N m).

Hooke's law: F = ke, where k is the spring constant (N/m) and e is extension (m). Only valid up to the limit of proportionality — beyond that, plastic deformation occurs.

Elastic PE: \(E_e = \tfrac{1}{2}ke^2\). Extension is squared — just like KE.

Common pitfalls:

  • Confusing mass (kg) and weight (N)
  • Using extension in cm instead of m in F = ke and E_e = ½ke²
  • Forgetting to square extension in the elastic PE equation

method_card.title: Speed, Acceleration and Motion Graphs
method_card.content:
Two equations and two graph types cover this lesson.

Speed: average speed (m/s) = distance (m) ÷ time (s).

Acceleration: a (m/s²) = change in speed (m/s) ÷ time (s). A negative value means deceleration.

Distance-time graph: gradient = speed. Steeper = faster. Horizontal = stationary.

Velocity-time graph: gradient = acceleration. Area under line = distance.

Common pitfalls:

  • Using final speed instead of change in speed for acceleration
  • Confusing the two graph types — a horizontal line means different things on each
  • Not using the correct area formula for the shape (triangle = ½ × base × height)

steps: Resultant force: F = ma (N = kg × m/s²). Rearrange to find a = F/m or m = F/a
Momentum (HT): p = mv (kg m/s). Conservation: total momentum before = total momentum after
Force from momentum change (HT): F = Δp ÷ Δt. Longer time = smaller force
Wave speed: v = f × λ. Rearrange to f = v/λ or λ = v/f
method_card.title: Newton's Laws, Momentum and Waves
method_card.content:
This lesson covers three equation families linked by Newton's laws.

F = ma: the resultant force equals mass × acceleration. If the resultant force is zero (Newton's first law), the object stays at rest or moves at constant speed.

Momentum (higher tier): p = mv (kg m/s). Momentum is conserved in a closed system. F = Δp/Δt — a longer collision time reduces peak force for the same change in momentum.

Wave speed: v = fλ. Units: m/s = Hz × m. All electromagnetic waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum.

Common pitfalls:

  • Not converting wavelength to metres before substituting into v = fλ
  • Confusing Newton's first law (zero resultant → constant speed) with Newton's second law (non-zero resultant → acceleration)

exam_context.frequency: High — F = ma and wave speed appear in most papers

gold.display: A crumple zone extends a collision from 0.05 s to 0.25 s. The driver's change in momentum is 900 kg m/s. Calculate the force WITH the crumple zone in newtons.

misconceptions.message: Impulse = F × t = 120 × 0.5 = 60 N s = Δp. v = Δp/m = 60/60 = 1 m/s.
Impulse = Δp = F × t = 60 N s. v = 60/60 = 1 m/s.

misconceptions.message: Total momentum before = 0. 0 = 2×3 + 3×v. v = −6/3 = −2 m/s. Magnitude = 2 m/s.
Momentum is conserved. Before = 0, so (2×3) + (3×v) = 0. v = −2 m/s.

steps: Find Mr: add up all Ar values in the formula, multiplying each by its subscript
Moles = mass (g) ÷ Mr. Rearrange: mass = moles × Mr; Mr = mass ÷ moles
Percentage by mass = (Ar × number of that atom ÷ Mr) × 100
Conservation of mass: in a closed system, total mass of reactants = total mass of products
method_card.title: Relative Formula Mass and Moles
method_card.content:
The mole is the 'bridge' between masses you can weigh and atoms you cannot see.

Mr calculation: List each element, multiply Ar by subscript, add up. H₂SO₄: (2×1) + 32 + (4×16) = 98.

Moles: moles = mass ÷ Mr. One mole has a mass in grams equal to Mr. One mole contains 6.0 × 10²³ particles.

Percentage by mass: (Ar × number of atoms ÷ Mr) × 100. Do not forget to multiply by 100.

Common pitfalls:

  • Not multiplying Ar by the subscript (e.g. treating H₂O as H + O instead of 2H + O)
  • Forgetting × 100 in the percentage calculation
  • Confusing open and closed systems when discussing mass changes

steps: Balance equations by changing coefficients only — never change formulae
Read off the mole ratio from the balanced equation coefficients
Convert given mass to moles: moles = mass ÷ Mr
Scale moles using the ratio, then convert back: mass = moles × Mr
method_card.title: Balancing Equations and Reacting Masses
method_card.content:
Reacting mass calculations always follow the same five steps.

Step 1: Write and balance the equation.

Step 2: Identify the mole ratio of the two substances you need.

Step 3: Convert the known mass to moles: moles = mass ÷ Mr.

Step 4: Use the ratio to find moles of the unknown.

Step 5: Convert back to mass: mass = moles × Mr.

Show all five steps clearly — method marks are available even if the final arithmetic is wrong.

Common pitfalls:

  • Changing a subscript instead of a coefficient when balancing
  • Skipping the mole ratio step
  • Basing calculations on the wrong reactant when a limiting reactant is specified

steps: List all bonds broken in reactants — multiply each bond energy by the number of that bond type
List all bonds made in products — multiply each bond energy by the number of that bond type
ΔH = energy to break bonds − energy released making bonds
Negative ΔH = exothermic; positive ΔH = endothermic
method_card.title: Bond Energy Calculations
method_card.content:
Every bond energy calculation has two sections: bonds broken and bonds made.

Bonds broken — always endothermic (energy in). List each bond type in the reactants and multiply by its count.

Bonds made — always exothermic (energy out). List each bond type in the products and multiply by its count. Remember to multiply by coefficients in the balanced equation.

Overall: ΔH = energy in − energy out. Negative = exothermic; positive = endothermic.

Common pitfalls:

  • Not counting all bonds — in 2H₂O there are 4 O-H bonds total (not 2)
  • Getting the sign wrong — bond breaking is energy IN, bond making is energy OUT
  • Using the wrong bond type (C=O double bond has higher energy than C-O single bond)

exam_context.frequency: Medium — bond energy questions appear regularly

gold.display: N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3. Bond energies: N≡N = 945, H-H = 436, N-H = 391 kJ/mol. Calculate ΔH.

misconceptions.message: Bonds broken: N≡N (945) + 3×H-H (1308) = 2253 kJ. Bonds made: 2×NH3 = 6 N-H bonds = 6×391 = 2346 kJ. ΔH = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ/mol.
2NH3 has 6 N-H bonds total (3 per molecule × 2 molecules).

gold.display: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. Bond energies: C-H = 412, O=O = 498, C=O = 743, O-H = 463 kJ/mol. Calculate ΔH.

misconceptions.message: Broken: 4×C-H (1648) + 2×O=O (996) = 2644. Made: 2×C=O (1486) + 4×O-H (1852) = wait: CO2 has 2 C=O bonds, 2×H2O has 4 O-H. Made = 2×743 + 4×463 = 1486+1852 = 3338. ΔH = 2644−3338 = −694. (Note: use values as given — answer depends on bond energies provided to the student.)
Bonds broken: CH4 has 4 C-H bonds. Each O2 has 1 O=O. Count all bonds carefully.

gold.display: A reaction has bonds broken = 1,200 kJ and ΔH = +300 kJ/mol. Calculate the energy released when bonds form in the products.

misconceptions.message: ΔH = energy in − energy out. 300 = 1200 − energy out. Energy out = 1200 − 300 = 900 kJ.

misconceptions.message: Bonds broken: H-H (436) + Cl-Cl (243) = 679 kJ.

bronze.display: H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. Bond energies: H-Cl = 432 kJ/mol. What is the total energy released making all bonds in the products (2 HCl molecules)?
bronze.equation_hint: Multiply bond energy by number of bonds made

misconceptions.message: 2 HCl molecules = 2 H-Cl bonds: 2 × 432 = 864 kJ.

misconceptions.message: Positive ΔH means more energy was absorbed breaking bonds than released making bonds — endothermic.

steps: Mean rate = quantity produced (or used) ÷ time. Units: cm³/s, g/s, or mol/dm³/s
From a graph: gradient at a point = instantaneous rate. Draw a tangent and calculate rise ÷ run
Concentration (g/dm³) = mass ÷ volume (dm³). Concentration (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume (dm³)
Always convert cm³ to dm³ before substituting into concentration equations (divide by 1,000)
method_card.title: Rates of Reaction and Concentrations
method_card.content:
Two key calculations: rate from data and concentration of a solution.

Mean rate: quantity produced (or used) ÷ time. The gradient of a rate-of-reaction graph gives the instantaneous rate at any point.

Concentration:

  • g/dm³ = mass (g) ÷ volume (dm³)
  • mol/dm³ = moles ÷ volume (dm³)
  • 1 dm³ = 1,000 cm³ — always convert before substituting

Common pitfalls:

  • Not converting cm³ to dm³ — the most common error in concentration calculations
  • Reading 'mean rate' from a specific point instead of total quantity ÷ total time
  • Confusing gradient (instantaneous rate) with overall mean rate

steps: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size (no units — it is a ratio)
To find actual size: actual = image size ÷ magnification
To find image size: image = actual size × magnification
Unit conversions: 1 mm = 1,000 µm; 1 µm = 1,000 nm. Multiply going to smaller units; divide going to larger.
method_card.title: Magnification and Unit Conversions
method_card.content:
The magnification formula has three forms — choose based on what you need to find.

Key rules:

  • Always ensure image size and actual size are in the same units before dividing
  • Magnification has NO units — it is a pure ratio
  • To go from mm → µm: multiply by 1,000. To go from µm → mm: divide by 1,000

Size reference points:

  • Plant cell: 10–100 µm
  • Animal cell: 10–30 µm
  • Mitochondrion: 1–10 µm
  • Bacterium: 1–10 µm
  • Virus: 20–300 nm

Common pitfalls:

  • Using different units for image and actual size (e.g. one in mm and the other in µm)
  • Forgetting to take the final unit conversion step
  • Multiplying by magnification instead of dividing when finding actual size

exam_context.frequency: Medium-High — magnification calculations appear regularly

steps: Write parental genotypes and identify the gametes each parent can produce
Draw the 2×2 Punnett square, placing gametes along the top and left side
Fill in the four cells by combining one allele from each parent
Count outcomes: genotype ratio (TT:Tt:tt) then phenotype ratio (dominant:recessive). Express probability as fraction, decimal or %
method_card.title: Punnett Squares and Genetic Probability
method_card.content:
Punnett squares predict the probability of each offspring genotype — they do not guarantee specific numbers.

Key rules:

  • Capital letter = dominant (shown in BB or Bb)
  • Lower-case letter = recessive (only shown in bb)
  • A Tt × Tt cross always gives 3 dominant : 1 recessive phenotype ratio
  • A Bb × bb cross always gives 1:1 dominant : recessive phenotype ratio

Probability from a Punnett square: count how many of the 4 cells show each outcome. If 2 out of 4 cells show Bb, the probability is 2/4 = 0.5 = 50%.

Common pitfalls:

  • Confusing genotype ratio (TT:Tt:tt = 1:2:1) with phenotype ratio (3:1)
  • Stating '1 in 3' instead of '1 in 4' — always count all 4 cells

Example structure:

Standard 2×2 Punnett square: Aa × Aa
Aa
AAAAa
aAaaa

exam_context.frequency: High — genetics appears in most biology papers

gold.display: A plant with genotype TT is crossed with a plant of unknown genotype that shows the tall (dominant) phenotype. Two offspring show the short (recessive) phenotype. What must the unknown parent's genotype be? Enter 1 for TT, 2 for Tt, or 3 for tt.
gold.question:
Use a Punnett square to test each possibility — the cross that produces tt offspring identifies the unknown parent.

A plant with genotype Tt is crossed with a plant of unknown genotype that shows the tall (dominant) phenotype. Two of the offspring show the short (recessive) phenotype. What must the unknown parent's genotype be? Enter 1 for TT, 2 for Tt, or 3 for tt.

misconceptions.message: If TT × TT, no short offspring are possible. If TT × Tt: Tt and TT offspring only (all tall). But short offspring appeared, so unknown parent must be Tt (not TT). Wait — TT × Tt gives TT and Tt only (all tall). For short offspring to appear, we need a tt parent. Reconsider: TT × tt gives all Tt (all tall). Tt × Tt gives 25% tt. So if short offspring appeared, the mystery parent must be Tt and the cross is Tt × Tt. Answer: Tt = 2.
For recessive offspring (tt) to appear, both parents must carry the t allele. TT parent provides only T. The unknown parent must provide t, so must be Tt.

gold.display: In humans, sex is determined by X and Y chromosomes. A couple have 4 children. Based on expected probability (50% each), how many would be expected to be female? Enter as a whole number.
gold.question: In humans, sex is determined by X and Y chromosomes. A couple have 4 children. Based on expected probability (50% each), how many would be expected to be girls?

misconceptions.message: Expected probability = 50% female. 50% of 4 = 2.

gold.display: A Tt × Tt cross produced 40 offspring. 28 were tall. Calculate the percentage that were tall.
gold.question: A Tt × Tt cross produced 40 offspring. 28 were tall. Calculate the percentage that were tall.

misconceptions.message: % tall = (28/40) × 100 = 70%. The expected ratio gives 75%, so actual results differ slightly due to random fertilisation.
Percentage = 28/40 × 100 = 70%.

bronze.question: In a Tt × Tt cross (T = tall, t = short, T dominant), what fraction of offspring show the tall phenotype? Enter as a decimal.
bronze.equation_hint: 3 out of 4 cells show tall phenotype (TT or Tt)

misconceptions.message: TT + Tt = 3 cells out of 4 show dominant phenotype = 3/4 = 0.75.

bronze.display: In a Tt × Tt cross, what percentage of offspring are expected to be homozygous recessive (tt)?
bronze.question: In a Tt × Tt cross, what percentage of offspring are expected to be homozygous recessive (tt)?

misconceptions.message: 1 cell out of 4 = tt = 1/4 = 25%.

steps: Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values
Estimated population = mean per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area)
Percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100
A positive result = increase; negative = decrease. Always divide by the ORIGINAL value
method_card.title: Sampling, Mean and Percentage Change
method_card.content:
Three calculations that appear regularly in ecology and data-handling questions.

Mean: add all values and divide by the count. Round sensibly — if data are whole numbers, one decimal place is usually fine.

Population estimate: mean per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area). Make sure you use the quadrat area (not just the number of quadrats).

Percentage change: % = (new − original) ÷ original × 100. Always use the original value in the denominator — using the new value is the most common error.

Common pitfalls:

  • Dividing by the new value instead of the original in percentage change
  • Not showing working for the mean (sum then divide)
  • Forgetting to account for quadrat size when estimating population

exam_context.frequency: Medium — data skills questions appear in most biology papers

gold.display: A student records dandelion counts in eight 0.5 m² quadrats in a 400 m² field: 5, 3, 6, 4, 5, 7, 4, 6. Estimate the total population.

misconceptions.message: Sum = 40. Mean = 5 per 0.5 m² quadrat. Number of quadrat-sized units = 400/0.5 = 800. Population = 5 × 800 = 4,000. Wait — re-check: mean is already per 0.5 m² quadrat, so population = 5 × (400/0.5) = 5 × 800 = 4,000.
Mean = 40/8 = 5 plants per quadrat. Quadrat area = 0.5 m². Units in field = 400/0.5 = 800. Population = 5 × 800 = 4,000.

gold.display: Mean seedling height was 3 cm at Week 1 and 7.8 cm at Week 4. Calculate the percentage change in height.

In a habitat survey, the mean number of wood lice per 1 m² quadrat was 12. The total habitat area is 800 m². Estimate the population. If next year the count gives a mean of 9 per quadrat, calculate the percentage change in estimated population.

bronze.display: A student records earthworm counts in 6 quadrats: 4, 7, 5, 6, 4, 8. Calculate the mean number per quadrat to 2 decimal places.
A population was 200 in Year 1 and 250 in Year 2. Calculate the percentage change.

misconceptions.message: % change = (250−200)/200 × 100 = 25%. Divide by the ORIGINAL value (200).

bronze.display: A population was 300 in Year 1 and 240 in Year 3. Calculate the percentage change (include sign).

misconceptions.message: % change = (240−300)/300 × 100 = −20%. The negative sign indicates a decrease.

Using the mean of 3 plants per quadrat (1 m² quadrats) in a 50 m² area, estimate the total population.
A plant was 5 cm tall in Week 1 and 15 cm tall in Week 4. Calculate the percentage change in height.

steps: Read the question — what quantity are you finding? (energy, power, speed, height?)
Recall the correct equation from memory
Convert all units (g→kg, mins→s, km/h→m/s, kJ→J)
Substitute values and calculate
State your answer with the correct unit (J, W, kJ, kW)
method_card.title: Energy: KE, GPE and Power
method_card.content:
This lesson covers five recall equations — none of them are on the equation sheet, so you need to know them from memory.

Approach for every calculation:

  1. Read the question — what are you asked to find?
  2. Identify the correct equation from memory
  3. List the values you're given and convert units if needed
  4. Substitute into the equation and calculate
  5. Write your answer with the correct unit

Common pitfalls:

  • Speed is squared in the KE equation — doubling speed quadruples KE
  • Convert time to seconds before using the power equation
  • Convert mass to kg (not grams) and speed to m/s
  • Use \(g = 9.8\) N/kg unless told otherwise
  • 1 kJ = 1000 J, 1 kW = 1000 W, 1 MW = 1,000,000 W

exam_context.frequency: Every exam — energy calculations appear on every Paper 1

gold.display: A skydiver of mass 75 kg falls from 4000 m to 3000 m. Calculate the speed they would reach if all the lost GPE converted to KE. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Use the height difference (4000 − 3000 = 1000 m), not the total height.

gold.display: A car of mass 1100 kg travels at 20 m/s. The driver brakes, and the car decelerates to 8 m/s. Calculate the work done by the brakes.
An electric motor has a power rating of 2.5 kW. It lifts a 80 kg object 6 m in 4 seconds. Calculate the efficiency of the motor. Give your answer as a percentage. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Useful output = mgh = 80 × 9.8 × 6 = 4704 J. Total input = Pt = 2500 × 4 = 10,000 J. Efficiency = 4704/10,000 × 100 = 47.04%.
Convert kW to W: 2.5 kW = 2500 W. Then total input energy = 2500 × 4 = 10,000 J.

gold.display: Two students climb the same flight of stairs (height 4 m). Student A has mass 50 kg and takes 5 seconds. Student B has mass 70 kg and takes 8 seconds. Which student has greater power output? Enter A or B.

misconceptions.message: Power A = mgh/t = (50 × 9.8 × 4)/5 = 392 W. Power B = (70 × 9.8 × 4)/8 = 343 W. Student A has greater power.

gold.display: A ball of mass 0.3 kg is dropped from a height of 10 m. It bounces back to a height of 6 m. Calculate the energy dissipated during the bounce. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: GPE before = 0.3 × 9.8 × 10 = 29.4 J. GPE after = 0.3 × 9.8 × 6 = 17.64 J. Energy dissipated = 29.4 − 17.64 = 11.76 J.

gold.display: A wind turbine generates 1.5 MW of power. How much energy does it transfer in one day? Give your answer in standard form.

bronze.display: A car has a mass of 1200 kg and travels at 15 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed first: 15² = 225. Then KE = ½ × 1200 × 225 = 135,000 J.
Don't forget the ½. KE = ½ × 1200 × 225 = 135,000 J, not 270,000 J.

bronze.display: A 0.5 kg ball is held 4 m above the ground. Calculate its gravitational potential energy. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A force of 50 N pushes a box 8 m along the floor. Calculate the work done.

misconceptions.message: Work done = force × distance = 50 × 8 = 400 J.

bronze.display: A kettle transfers 180,000 J of energy in 3 minutes. Calculate its power in watts.

misconceptions.message: Convert minutes to seconds first: 3 min = 180 s. P = 180,000 ÷ 180 = 1000 W.

bronze.display: A runner of mass 60 kg sprints at 8 m/s. Calculate their kinetic energy.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed: 8² = 64. KE = ½ × 60 × 64 = 1920 J.

bronze.display: A bag of mass 3 kg is lifted onto a shelf 2.5 m high. Calculate the GPE gained. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A motor does 5000 J of work in 20 seconds. Calculate its power.

misconceptions.message: Power = energy ÷ time = 5000 ÷ 20 = 250 W. Don't multiply.

bronze.display: Which equation would you use to calculate the energy stored by an object lifted above the ground?

misconceptions.message: An object above the ground has gravitational PE. Use Eₚ = mgh. KE is for moving objects.

silver.display: A cyclist and bike have a combined mass of 80 kg and travel at 12 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy in kJ.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed first: 12² = 144. Then ½ × 80 × 144 = 5760 J = 5.76 kJ.

silver.display: A 60 W light bulb is left on for 2 hours. Calculate the energy transferred in kJ.

misconceptions.message: Convert hours to seconds: 2 h = 7200 s. E = Pt = 60 × 7200 = 432,000 J = 432 kJ.

silver.display: A crane lifts a 400 kg load to a height of 15 m. Calculate the work done by the crane. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: First find the weight: W = mg = 400 × 9.8 = 3920 N. Then work done = Fs = 3920 × 15 = 58,800 J.

silver.display: A car of mass 900 kg accelerates from rest to 30 m/s. Calculate the work done on the car.

misconceptions.message: Work done = change in KE = ½ × 900 × 30² = ½ × 900 × 900 = 405,000 J.
Don't forget to square the speed: 30² = 900. KE = ½ × 900 × 900 = 405,000 J.

silver.display: A 1500 W motor lifts a 50 kg mass. How high can it lift the mass in 10 seconds? Give your answer to 1 d.p. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A 200 g tennis ball is served at 50 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

misconceptions.message: Convert grams to kg: 200 g = 0.2 kg. KE = ½ × 0.2 × 50² = ½ × 0.2 × 2500 = 250 J.

worked_examples.question: A ball of mass 0.4 kg is thrown at a speed of 10 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
A crane lifts a 250 kg beam to a height of 12 m in 30 seconds. Calculate the power of the crane. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

Step 2 — Set GPE = KE and rearrange for v

steps: Identify the useful output and the total input (energy or power)
Check you're not accidentally using wasted energy as the useful output
Divide: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input
Multiply by 100 if the question asks for a percentage
Check your answer is less than 1 (or 100%) — if not, you've divided the wrong way
method_card.title: Efficiency and Energy Resources
method_card.content:
Efficiency tells you how good a device is at converting energy into the form you want. It's a recall equation — not on the equation sheet.

Key strategy:

  1. Identify the useful output energy (or power) — this is the form you actually want
  2. Identify the total input energy (or power) — everything that goes in
  3. Divide useful by total to get efficiency as a decimal
  4. Multiply by 100 if the question asks for a percentage

Critical rules:

  • Efficiency can never exceed 1 (or 100%) — if your answer is above this, you've divided the wrong way round
  • Wasted energy = total input − useful output
  • You can use either energy values or power values — never mix them
  • On Sankey diagrams, the width of each arrow is proportional to the energy — read the scale carefully

Common exam pitfall: Questions sometimes give you wasted energy instead of useful energy. Always check which one you've been given before dividing.

exam_context.frequency: Very common — efficiency appears in almost every Paper 1

gold.display: A crane motor with an efficiency of 0.75 lifts a 120 kg steel beam to a height of 20 m. Calculate the total electrical energy input to the motor. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Useful output = GPE = mgh = 120 × 9.8 × 20 = 23,520 J. Total input = useful ÷ efficiency = 23,520 ÷ 0.75 = 31,360 J.
Don't multiply useful by efficiency. Total input = useful output ÷ efficiency.

gold.display: A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates from rest to 25 m/s. The engine has an efficiency of 0.30. Calculate the total chemical energy released from the fuel.

misconceptions.message: First find KE gained: ½ × 1200 × 25² = ½ × 1200 × 625 = 375,000 J. This is the useful output. Total input = 375,000 ÷ 0.30 = 1,250,000 J.
Remember to square the speed: 25² = 625, not 25 × 2 = 50.

gold.display: A solar panel converts sunlight into 240 W of useful electrical power. The panel is 20% efficient. The Sun delivers 800 W/m² to the panel. Calculate the area of the panel.

misconceptions.message: Total input power = useful ÷ efficiency = 240 ÷ 0.20 = 1200 W. Area = total power ÷ power per m² = 1200 ÷ 800 = 1.5 m².
First find total power input, then divide by the solar intensity to find the area.

gold.display: A pump with a power rating of 600 W and an efficiency of 0.70 lifts water to a height of 8 m for 5 minutes. Calculate the mass of water lifted. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Remember to account for the efficiency — only 70% of the input energy lifts the water.

gold.display: A student compares two kettles. Kettle A is 88% efficient and takes 3 minutes to boil using 2000 W. Kettle B is 95% efficient and takes 3 minutes to boil using 1800 W. Which kettle transfers more useful energy to the water? Enter A or B.

misconceptions.message: Kettle A: useful = 0.88 × 2000 × 180 = 316,800 J. Kettle B: useful = 0.95 × 1800 × 180 = 307,800 J. Despite B being more efficient, A transfers more useful energy because of its higher power rating.

gold.display: Which statement about efficiency is correct?
options: A more powerful device is always more efficient
Efficiency can be greater than 100% if the device is very good
Wasted energy is eventually transferred to the surroundings, increasing the temperature
Renewable energy sources always have higher efficiency than fossil fuels

misconceptions.message: Efficiency can never exceed 100% (conservation of energy). Power and efficiency are different things. Wasted energy always ends up heating the surroundings — this is correct.

bronze.display: A heater receives 2000 J of electrical energy and converts 1600 J to heat for the room. Calculate the efficiency of the heater.

misconceptions.message: Divide useful by total, not total by useful. Efficiency = 1600 ÷ 2000 = 0.8.
Useful output (1600 J) is the heat for the room. Efficiency = 1600/2000 = 0.8.

bronze.display: A motor has an input energy of 500 J and a useful output of 350 J. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = 350/500 = 0.7. Multiply by 100 to get a percentage: 0.7 × 100 = 70%.

bronze.display: An LED bulb has an input power of 10 W and a useful light output of 7 W. Calculate the efficiency.

misconceptions.message: You can use power values directly. Efficiency = useful power ÷ total power = 7 ÷ 10 = 0.7.

bronze.display: A car engine receives 40,000 J of chemical energy from fuel and converts 12,000 J to kinetic energy. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = useful ÷ total = 12,000 ÷ 40,000 = 0.3 = 30%. Don't divide 40,000 by 12,000.

bronze.display: A kettle is 90% efficient. It receives 200,000 J of electrical energy. Calculate the useful heat energy transferred to the water.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: useful output = efficiency × total input = 0.9 × 200,000 = 180,000 J. Convert 90% to 0.9 first.

bronze.display: A power station has an efficiency of 0.35. The total input power is 800 MW. Calculate the useful electrical power output in MW.

misconceptions.message: Useful output = efficiency × total input = 0.35 × 800 = 280 MW.
Both values are already in MW, so the answer stays in MW. No conversion needed.

bronze.display: A Sankey diagram shows a light bulb receiving 80 J of electrical energy. The useful light output arrow has a width of 8 J. Calculate the wasted energy.

misconceptions.message: Wasted energy = total input − useful output = 80 − 8 = 72 J. Energy is conserved.

bronze.display: Which of these devices is the most efficient?
options: Device A: 500 J in, 200 J useful out
Device B: 400 J in, 300 J useful out
Device C: 1000 J in, 600 J useful out
Device D: 200 J in, 50 J useful out

misconceptions.message: Calculate each: A = 200/500 = 0.40, B = 300/400 = 0.75, C = 600/1000 = 0.60, D = 50/200 = 0.25. Device B is the most efficient at 75%.

silver.display: A motor receives 5000 J of electrical energy. It wastes 1500 J as heat and 500 J as sound. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

misconceptions.message: Useful = total − all wasted = 5000 − 1500 − 500 = 3000 J. Efficiency = 3000/5000 = 0.6 = 60%.
Remember to subtract ALL the wasted energies (heat and sound) from the input.

silver.display: A wind turbine has an efficiency of 0.40. In one hour it generates 720 kJ of useful electrical energy. Calculate the total energy input from the wind in kJ.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency = 720 ÷ 0.40 = 1800 kJ.
Don't multiply: total input = 720 ÷ 0.40 = 1800 kJ. The total must be MORE than the useful output.

silver.display: A gas boiler is 92% efficient and provides 46,000 J of useful heat energy. Calculate the total energy wasted by the boiler.

misconceptions.message: First find total input: 46,000 ÷ 0.92 = 50,000 J. Then wasted = total − useful = 50,000 − 46,000 = 4000 J.

silver.display: A hydroelectric power station converts the GPE of falling water into electricity. 8000 kg of water falls through 50 m every second. The station has an efficiency of 0.85. Calculate the useful power output. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: GPE per second = mgh = 8000 × 9.8 × 50 = 3,920,000 W. Useful output = efficiency × input power = 0.85 × 3,920,000 = 3,332,000 W.
Since the water falls every second, mgh gives energy per second — which is power in watts.

silver.display: An electric drill has a power rating of 750 W and an efficiency of 0.60. Calculate the power wasted as heat and sound.

misconceptions.message: Useful = efficiency × total = 0.60 × 750 = 450 W. Wasted = 750 − 450 = 300 W.
Find useful power first (efficiency × input), then subtract from total to get wasted power.

silver.display: A Sankey diagram for a coal power station shows 1000 MJ input. The useful electricity arrow is 350 MJ and the cooling tower waste arrow is 500 MJ. Calculate the energy lost through other waste pathways.

misconceptions.message: Total in = all out. Other waste = 1000 − 350 − 500 = 150 MJ. Energy is always conserved.

steps.label: Step 1 — Find the useful power output

worked_examples.question: A motor has an input power of 500 W and wastes 175 W as heat and sound. Calculate its efficiency as a percentage.

steps.label: Step 1 — Calculate the useful output (GPE gained)
